yours:
Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
At midnight there came a message from Ryan, desiring that we might converse together upon a matter of consequence; and its purport was so little doubtful, that I understood it at once.

On the following day we met at a coffee-house in the town, where I found him already seated, his eyes fixed in apparent occupation upon his small instrument; nor did his countenance fail to discover an uneasy agitation. He began by declaring himself unprepared for any serious engagement; and with many assurances that the fault lay entirely in his own character, and by no means in mine, he laboured to soften what could not be made agreeable.

Though my heart was full, and tears were very near, I preserved sufficient composure to withhold them, and could only answer him by a silent inclination of the head and an assent of the most brief civility. I then walked home through the rain; and arriving at my lodgings, I sought what consolation was to be derived from devouring a whole pint of ice cream.

The friend who shared my room considered my distress to be quite beyond reason; and perhaps she was not mistaken. Yet the wound was not the less real.

lessons: The chief difference lies in the architecture of the period and the vocabulary of judgement: where your draft gives rapid, unadorned actions in fragments, Austen gathers related thoughts into balanced periods joined by semicolons, and filters emotion through social propriety and composure. Practise replacing modern abbreviations of feeling with abstract nouns of judgement (“composure”, “civility”, “mortification”) and expressing distress through conduct rather than mere announcement.

outline.gist: A late message from Ryan signaling the end.
Meeting at the coffee shop and his awkward speech.
Restrained reaction and solitary indulgence at home.
Roommate's dismissal and lingering hurt.

plan.why: Austen establishes the arrival of intelligence and the immediate moral apprehension in a single balanced period.
plan.gist: The midnight summons and its unmistakable meaning.

plan.why: Grouping the visual conduct and the reported speeches lets his evasive civility unfold with ironic weight.
plan.gist: The meeting, his nervous distraction, and his apologetic refusal of commitment.
The narrator's struggle for composure and solitary retreat in the rain.
plan.why: Restraint in public followed by private comfort is Austen's characteristic manner of treating wounded affection.

plan.gist: The companion's rational critique and the final acknowledgement of pain.
plan.why: Closing with a balanced qualification followed by a short, firm verdict delivers the emotional landing cleanly.

faults.quote: “at a coffee-house in the town”
faults.why: This weakens the specific setting “a coffee shop downtown.” “In the town” is broader and does not preserve the downtown detail.

faults.quote: “his eyes fixed in apparent occupation upon his small instrument”
faults.why: Ryan was specifically scrolling on his phone. “Small instrument” obscures both the phone and the scrolling, dropping a concrete action rather than clearly translating it.

faults.quote: “the fault lay entirely in his own character”
faults.why: The original says that he was not ready for something serious and gives the conventional “it was him” reassurance. Calling it a fault in his “character” makes the statement more morally accusatory and changes its degree and implication.

faults.quote: “The friend who shared my room”
faults.why: A roommate is recast as merely a friend who shares the narrator’s room. That alters the stated relationship and unnecessarily adds “friend.”

faults.quote: “perhaps she was not mistaken”
faults.why: The source does not establish the roommate’s gender. The added pronoun invents a fact.

faults.quote: “his small instrument”
faults.why: This is conspicuously evasive pseudo-period diction rather than Austenian idiom. It makes the modern object into a riddle instead of integrating the fact with Austen-like social observation.

faults.quote: “his eyes fixed in apparent occupation upon his small instrument”
faults.why: The phrase is cumbersome and unintentionally comic: “apparent occupation” and “small instrument” do not naturally communicate that he is nervously scrolling on a phone.

faults.quote: “I sought what consolation was to be derived from devouring a whole pint of ice cream”
faults.why: The elaborate circumlocution reads as generalized period parody. Austen can be ironic and formal, but this phrasing calls attention to its costume rather than producing her precise, socially observant narration.

faults.quote: “Paragraph 2: (no notes)” / “Paragraph 3: (no notes)” / “Paragraph 4: (no notes)”
faults.why: The rewrite makes numerous consequential choices—turning the phone into a “small instrument,” recasting the breakup explanation as a character fault, changing “roommate,” and adding a gender—but the notes neither identify nor justify them.

faults.quote: “cites Mansfield Park, ch. 32, ¶ 1”
faults.why: A single citation is attached only to the first paragraph’s balanced period. It does not support the broader Austen claims in the structural commentary or help the writer study the major techniques used in the remaining rewrite.

faults.quote: “Practise replacing modern abbreviations of feeling with abstract nouns of judgement”
faults.why: This is too broad and risks teaching imitation by antique abstraction. It gives examples such as “mortification,” but does not show how to preserve the draft’s exact emotional intensity while using a concrete Austenian device such as free indirect judgement, dialogue, or contrast between outward conduct and inward feeling.

faults.quote: “Austen gathers related thoughts into balanced periods joined by semicolons”
faults.why: The lesson reduces Austen’s method to punctuation and longer sentences. It should distinguish purposeful balance and ironic qualification from merely adding semicolons, especially since the rewrite’s most awkward phrases arise from ornamental circumlocution.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the basic sequence and emotional arc, and its story structure remains effective. However, it repeatedly substitutes vague pseudo-regency diction for concrete facts, changes a few details, and provides too little annotation to make those choices useful as teaching.

yours:
A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family took possession of the house adjoining ours at the close of last week; and their arrival was marked by a vast cart of goods, and the appearance of two little children. The father appeared perfectly agreeable and good-humoured; but the lady his sister, who had accompanied him, was distant, and not a little unapproachable in her air.

My mother immediately prepared a plate of biscuits for their reception, impatient to learn every circumstance of their condition; and she was not long in setting about her inquiries. She was determined to know whence they had come, what profession was pursued, and whether they were constant in their attendance at church.

It appeared, at length, that the father was in the law, and entirely single—or rather parted from his wife, as the story went. My mother’s countenance instantly assumed that peculiar look which I knew too well; for her imagination was already at work, and having for years made my establishment her chief business, she saw in our new neighbour an opportunity not to be neglected.

rows.text: A new family took possession of the house adjoining ours at the close of last week; and their arrival was marked by a vast cart of goods, and the appearance of two little children. The father appeared perfectly agreeable and good-humoured; but the lady his sister, who had accompanied him, was distant, and not a little unapproachable in her air.

notes.text: Your opening paragraph introduces a mother who is standoffish, yet your final paragraph reveals the father to be single and divorced, meaning both parents cannot inhabit the house together while leaving him eligible for courtship. I made the reserved lady his sister, echoing the dynamic of Mr. Bingley and his haughty sisters in Pride and Prejudice, which removes the domestic contradiction while preserving the single status essential to your mother’s matchmaking.
notes.after: the lady his sister, who had accompanied him, was distant, and not a little unapproachable in her air

notes.text: The narrator provides an ironic summary of the mother’s matchmaking design, translating maternal ambition into a calculation of matrimonial advantage.
notes.after: she saw in our new neighbour an opportunity not to be neglected

lessons: Where your draft relies on short, detached declarations, Austen weaves observations together through balanced periodic clauses and abstract nouns of judgement. In rendering your mother’s overture as being “impatient to learn every circumstance of their condition”, the narrative exposes social curiosity beneath neighbourly manners; while characterizing her habitual designs by noting that “having for years made my establishment her chief business, she saw in our new neighbour an opportunity not to be neglected”, dry irony elevates an ordinary matrimonial scheme into comedy. Practise sustaining a thought across semicolons so that each detail gathers weight before the concluding verdict arrives.

outline.gist: A new family moves in next door with a truck and children, featuring an agreeable father and an aloof woman.
The narrator's mother brings them baked goods to interrogate their background and habits.
The father is revealed to be an unattached lawyer, reawakening the mother's marital hopes for her daughter.

plan.why: Austen establishes social arrivals through balanced periodic periods, clarifying the domestic relations to prepare for the marital comedy.
plan.gist: The arrival of the new household next door is described, balancing the father's affability against the sister's reserve.

plan.why: The author renders curiosity through abstract nouns of circumstance, showing how neighbouring civilities conceal inquisitiveness.
plan.gist: The mother uses a domestic gift to pursue an inquisitive social reconnaissance.

plan.why: The narrator turns to free indirect awareness and dry irony to puncture the mother's longstanding ambition to see her child settled.
plan.gist: The discovery of the father's single state and profession prompts the mother's matrimonial schemes.

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mother — "The mom is kind of standoffish" — and your last says the dad "is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced." As written, both sentences describe the same household, so the household has a mother and its father is single, which cannot both be true of the same family at the same time.
sense.quote: The mom is kind of standoffish. ... It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.
sense.resolution: Make the standoffish woman something other than the children's mother, since the father is the single (divorced) parent: "The woman who lives there seems kind of standoffish" — she might be his sister, his mother, or a girlfriend — or make clear the mother does not live there: "The mom isn't around; the dad seems nice." That keeps both sentences true of the same household and keeps the matchmaking turn, which needs a single man next door, intact.

faults.quote: "a vast cart of goods"
faults.why: This replaces the family’s "huge truck" with a cart and shifts the emphasis from the vehicle itself to its cargo. A period adaptation may be tempting, but the stated fidelity standard requires the fact to be retained.

faults.quote: "who had accompanied him"
faults.why: The draft says that a family moved in; it does not say that the reserved woman merely accompanied the father. This adds a specific circumstance to the sister solution which is not needed to mend the contradiction.

faults.quote: "The father appeared perfectly agreeable and good-humoured"
faults.why: "Seems nice" is a mild, tentative judgement. "Perfectly agreeable and good-humoured" makes the narrator more certain and raises the warmth of the judgement.

faults.quote: "she was not long in setting about her inquiries"
faults.why: The original establishes the mother’s wish to discover the neighbours’ details, expressed through baking cookies; it does not state that she immediately questioned them. The rewrite adds an enacted interrogation.

faults.quote: "as the story went"
faults.why: "It turns out" presents the information as established. This phrase recasts the divorce as neighbourhood hearsay, changing the narrator’s degree of certainty.

faults.quote: "the lady his sister"
faults.why: Without commas, this is syntactically awkward and briefly obscure. "The lady, his sister," would be clearer and more idiomatic even in an Austen-like period.

faults.quote: "entirely single—or rather parted from his wife"
faults.why: The correction does not quite work: a divorced man can still be described as single, while "parted from his wife" can suggest separation rather than divorce. The original’s comic correction distinguishes never-married from divorced; "unmarried—or rather, divorced" would preserve that distinction more cleanly.

faults.quote: "Clauses balanced in one period ... — cites Emma, ch. 25, ¶ 6"
faults.why: The note identifies a broad technique, but it gives no quotation or explanation of the cited Austen passage showing the comparable construction. A chapter-and-paragraph reference, especially one dependent on edition, is not enough to make the source useful to the learner.

faults.quote: "Understatement and litotes: ‘not a little unapproachable in her air’"
faults.why: The note accurately labels the device but does not explain what the understatement does here: it converts the draft’s casual "standoffish" into socially observant, guarded judgement. The writer is told the name of a move rather than how to reuse it.

faults.quote: "Liberty taken: The narrator provides an ironic summary"
faults.why: This reports the final ironic expansion, but not other material liberties, including changing the truck to a cart, adding that the sister "accompanied him," and making the mother actively conduct inquiries. Those changes should be acknowledged so the writer can distinguish voice effects from altered facts.

faults.quote: "Practise sustaining a thought across semicolons"
faults.why: This is a concrete exercise, but it risks reducing Austen’s effect to punctuation. The lesson should also teach the more transferable underlying move: arrange neutral observation, social inference, and an ironic final judgement so that the sentence’s final clause delivers the comic verdict.

judge.verdict: The rewrite handles the draft’s parental-status contradiction well and has a convincing Austenian social-comic surface. Its main weaknesses are unreported factual embellishments, a few awkward formulations, and notes that name techniques more readily than they demonstrate and teach them.

yours:
Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
My dear Friends,

I write in haste to give you notice that our endeavour, which had been fixed for Tuesday, is now deferred till Thursday. The gentlemen of the law have not yet signified their approval of the paper of charges; and I consider it by no means prudent that we should proceed while their sanction is withheld.

You will have the goodness to complete your respective parts of the packet by Wednesday at noon; and should any difficulty hinder your progress, I must entreat to be informed of it today, rather than tomorrow.

Accept my best thanks, and believe me ever yours, Sam.

I write in haste to give you notice that our endeavour, which had been fixed for Tuesday, is now deferred till Thursday. The gentlemen of the law have not yet signified their approval of the paper of charges; and I consider it by no means prudent that we should proceed while their sanction is withheld.

notes.text: Renders the informal heading and opening tag as an epistolary formula that justifies brevity and dispatch.
notes.after: I write in haste

rows.text: You will have the goodness to complete your respective parts of the packet by Wednesday at noon; and should any difficulty hinder your progress, I must entreat to be informed of it today, rather than tomorrow.

notes.after: You will have the goodness to complete your respective parts of the packet by Wednesday at noon; and should any difficulty hinder your progress, I must entreat to be informed of it today, rather than tomorrow.

rows.text: Accept my best thanks, and believe me ever yours, Sam.

lessons: The chief difference lies in the elevation of colloquial office jargon into the polished decorum of Regency epistolary prose. Instead of blunt fragments and modern technical shorthand, the rewrite employs balanced periods joined by semicolons, litotes (“by no means prudent”), and abstract nouns of conduct (“sanction”, “notice”). Practise framing administrative demands with formulas of civil expectation (“You will have the goodness to…”) and expressing urgent contingencies through balanced conditional clauses.

outline.gist: Salutation to the group
The launch is postponed from Tuesday to Thursday
Legal has not signed off on the pricing page
Submit sections of the deck by Wednesday noon and report impediments today
Thanks and sign-off

plan.gist: Salutation to the recipients
plan.why: A civil epistolary address opens the communication in proper form.
Stating the deferral and immediately grounding it in legal sanction provides clarity through balanced periodic syntax.
plan.gist: Postponement of the enterprise and its legal reason
Instruction for the completion of papers and reporting of obstacles
plan.why: Joining the deadline and the warning into a single period softens a direct command into civil urgency.
A brief, warm epistolary close maintains the brevity of the original while preserving decorum.
plan.gist: Acknowledgment and signature

faults.quote: The gentlemen of the law
faults.why: “Legal” may be a department or function, not a group of male lawyers. The rewrite adds gendered persons and a particular institutional interpretation not present in the email.

faults.quote: the paper of charges
faults.why: This weakens the specific fact that Legal has not approved a “pricing page.” A paper of charges can mean an invoice, a schedule of fees, or even an accusation; it does not securely preserve either the web-page form or the pricing context.

faults.quote: I consider it by no means prudent that we should proceed
faults.why: The original states Sam’s direct preference not to ship without approval. This recasts it as a generalized judgement of prudence and replaces the concrete act of shipping with the vaguer “proceed,” slightly softening and abstracting the intended instruction.

faults.quote: The gentlemen of the law ... the paper of charges
faults.why: These substitutions are broadly faux-Regency rather than distinctively Austenian. They pile up historical-sounding labels where Austen’s letters are often more direct and socially precise; the result sounds costumed and makes the modern work matter less intelligible.

faults.quote: the paper of charges
faults.why: The phrase is ambiguous and slightly comic in this setting: it may suggest legal charges or an account of expenses rather than a pricing page awaiting Legal’s approval.

faults.quote: Accept my best thanks, and believe me ever yours, Sam.
faults.why: For a team work email, “ever yours” overstates personal intimacy and turns a conventional sign-off into a private-letter valediction. It is not a natural equivalent of the original’s simple “Thanks.”

faults.quote: [liberty] Liberty taken: Renders the informal heading and opening tag as an epistolary formula that justifies brevity and dispatch.
faults.why: The note is imprecise: the source has a greeting, “Hi team,” not an “opening tag,” and it does not identify the exact rewritten wording or explain why the substantial change is necessary. It also supplies no source for the alleged epistolary practice.

faults.quote: Paragraph 2
faults.why: The paragraph labels do not clearly correspond to the displayed rewrite. The note about the opening belongs to the salutation/opening paragraph, while the quoted balanced request appears in the second body paragraph; the later “Paragraph 4” has no visible corresponding paragraph.

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: No note reports the consequential factual substitutions “gentlemen of the law,” “paper of charges,” “endeavour,” and “packet.” In particular, “paper of charges” creates a real clarity risk and should have been either avoided or explicitly reported as a sense mending.

faults.quote: Instead of blunt fragments and modern technical shorthand
faults.why: This inaccurately characterizes the original. Apart from the conventional greeting and sign-off, it consists of clear complete sentences; “deck” and “blocked” are workplace terms, not merely “technical shorthand.” The lesson therefore teaches by dismissing sound plain prose rather than showing a selective, reusable transformation.

faults.quote: Practise framing administrative demands with formulas of civil expectation
faults.why: The advice usefully names a formula but does not warn that such elevation can obscure essential operational nouns. It should connect the lesson to this example by preserving concrete anchors such as the launch, pricing page, deck, and deadline while changing cadence and politeness.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the email’s overall sequence, deadlines, and two requests, and its structure is appropriately retained. Its main weaknesses are imprecise faux-period substitutions—especially for the pricing page—and notes that neither account for those changes nor provide sufficiently accurate, practical teaching.

yours:
Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Our town would consult its own convenience by closing Main Street against carriages at the close of every week; for the placing of such machines in the midst of the place is become an intolerable grievance, and the pavements are far too narrow for children’s carriages. Other places have already ventured on the experiment; and their shops are found to flourish beyond all former example.

A few of the tradesmen will not fail to complain that buyers cannot reach them; but they will soon find the alteration no very great hardship, when they recollect that the greater part of the world walk from the coach-house at all events. We ought certainly to make trial of the scheme during the present summer.

Other places have already ventured on the experiment; and their shops are found to flourish beyond all former example.

notes.after: for the placing of such machines in the midst of the place is become an intolerable grievance, and the pavements are far too narrow for children’s carriages.

notes.text: The narrator frames a civic recommendation in terms of collective propriety and ease, lending Austen’s measured decorum to a bare imperative.
notes.after: would consult its own convenience

rows.text: A few of the tradesmen will not fail to complain that buyers cannot reach them; but they will soon find the alteration no very great hardship, when they recollect that the greater part of the world walk from the coach-house at all events. We ought certainly to make trial of the scheme during the present summer.

notes.text: Brings together your paragraphs 2 and 3.

notes.after: they will soon find the alteration no very great hardship

lessons: Where your draft relies on casual hyperbole and staccato assertions, Austen marshals balanced periods and precise nouns of judgement to give persuasion moral weight. Notice how “is become an intolerable grievance” translates informal frustration into composed civic judgement, while “they will soon find the alteration no very great hardship” disarms an anticipated objection through understated litotes. Practise joining objections to their practical answers within a single periodic sentence, allowing measured syntax rather than abrupt dismissal to carry your argument.

outline.gist: close Main Street on weekends
parking difficulties and narrow sidewalks
other towns have succeeded
business owners will complain
they will adapt
most people already walk from the garage
try the measure this summer

plan.gist: recommending the closure of Main Street to carriages at the end of the week, supported by the inconvenience of vehicles, the narrowness of the walks, and the precedent of neighbouring places
plan.why: Austen connects a civic proposal directly to its material justifications and outside precedent within sustained, balanced periods, establishing decorum and evidence before entertaining objections.

plan.gist: answering the anticipated discontent of tradesmen with the reality of walking habits, and concluding with a prompt trial of the scheme this summer
plan.why: Uniting the objection, its practical refutation, and the final appeal prevents fragmentary modern paragraphs and allows the concluding verdict to land with decisive authority.

faults.quote: “for the placing of such machines in the midst of the place is become an intolerable grievance”
faults.why: This does not preserve the stated parking problem. The draft says that finding parking downtown is difficult; this recasts the problem as the objectionable presence or placement of vehicles in town. Those are materially different grounds for closure.

faults.quote: “the greater part of the world walk from the coach-house at all events”
faults.why: A downtown garage is presumably a public parking facility from which customers walk. A “coach-house” is ordinarily a private building for storing coaches, so the rewrite makes the practical rebuttal unclear and does not support the claim about customers’ access.

faults.quote: “the greater part of the world”
faults.why: The draft’s “most people” concerns the relevant local shoppers. “The greater part of the world” turns a local observation into a sweeping claim about humanity; even as Austenian hyperbole, it alters the scope of the evidence.

faults.quote: “at the close of every week”
faults.why: This is not a clear equivalent of closing the street “on weekends.” It can mean a closure at the end of each week, rather than throughout Saturday and Sunday.

faults.quote: “such machines”
faults.why: This reads as a conspicuous historical substitution for cars rather than Austen’s more natural vocabulary for vehicles, especially when “carriages” has already been used. The circumlocution draws attention to the costume instead of sounding organically Austenian.

faults.quote: “cites Pride and Prejudice, ch. 43, ¶ 57”
faults.why: The note presents a highly precise citation for the general device of balanced clauses but supplies no quoted parallel or explanation of the connection. A chapter-and-paragraph citation is also not readily verifiable across editions; it does not adequately demonstrate that this particular move derives from the cited passage.

faults.quote: “Paragraph 1 (renders the writer’s ¶1)”
faults.why: The notes do not report the consequential change from a shortage/difficulty of parking to an objection to vehicles being placed in the street, nor do they identify the substitution of a public garage with a coach-house. These are sense-affecting liberties, not merely stylistic ones.

faults.quote: “other towns have succeeded” / “precedent of neighbouring places”
faults.why: The structural explanation calls the other places “neighbouring,” though neither the draft nor the rewrite establishes that they are nearby. The explanatory account introduces a factual qualification that is unsupported by the source.

faults.quote: “your draft relies on casual hyperbole”
faults.why: “Parking downtown is a nightmare” is informal emphasis, but calling it hyperbole oversimplifies the writer’s concrete usability complaint. The lesson also does not show how to preserve that specific practical fact while adopting Austen’s measured register.

judge.verdict: The rewrite has a credible Austen-like surface and a stronger two-part argument, but its central practical reason is changed: parking difficulty becomes a complaint about vehicles themselves. The unreported garage/coach-house substitution further weakens the rebuttal, so the stylistic gains do not preserve the writer’s meaning closely enough.

yours:
I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.

When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana sent an excuse to break our appointment for dinner, I felt not the smallest mortification; I was, in truth, sensible only of relief. Through the whole of the week I had dreaded the engagement, and of such a reluctance I had very little reason to be proud.

I assured her that it was of no consequence, and that we must fix upon another day to dine together; but I do not believe we ever shall.

lessons: Where your draft relies on blunt modern shorthand, Austen translates social discomfort into moral judgement and periodic balance. By rendering the absence of distress through litotes and abstract nouns in “felt not the smallest mortification” and “sensible only of relief,” the prose measures feeling by decorum rather than raw sensation. Practise balancing outward civility against private truth in a single period, letting reported politeness be punctured by a deflating closing clause such as “; but I do not believe we ever shall.”

outline.gist: Dana cancels the dinner and the narrator feels relief rather than distress
Narrator admits to dreading the dinner all week with some shame
Narrator politely reassures Dana and proposes meeting another time
Narrator privately acknowledges that the meeting will never happen

plan.why: Austen opens by balancing the social disruption against the private satisfaction in a single period, framing the lack of distress through litotes and moral judgement.
plan.gist: Dana cancels the dinner and the narrator receives the excuse with relief
Narrator confesses to having dreaded the visit all week, humbled by the reluctance
plan.why: Leading with the duration of the anxiety allows the moral evaluation of the feeling to conclude the period with propriety.
Polite speech is rendered indirectly to capture social decorum, while the semicolon introduces a dry, deflating clause that exposes the insincerity of the promise.
plan.gist: Narrator renders the polite compliance in reported speech, deflated by a private verdict

faults.quote: “When Dana sent an excuse to break our appointment for dinner”
faults.why: The draft says only that Dana cancelled. “sent an excuse” adds both a mode of communication and the implication that Dana offered an excuse; neither is supplied. “appointment” also makes the dinner sound more formal than the original’s ordinary social plan.

faults.quote: “I felt not the smallest mortification”
faults.why: “Mortification” in Austen commonly denotes wounded pride, humiliation, or chagrin, rather than the full ordinary meaning of “upset.” The original says the narrator was not upset at all, without specifying that pride or embarrassment was absent. This narrows and slightly redirects the feeling.

faults.quote: “break our appointment for dinner”
faults.why: The phrase is stiffer and more bureaucratic than characteristically Austenian social narration. Austen more naturally uses terms such as an engagement, invitation, visit, or party; “break our appointment” sounds like modern formal scheduling language in period costume.

faults.quote: “cites Persuasion, ch. 21, ¶ 98” / “cites Sense and Sensibility, ch. 41, ¶ 4” / “cites Mansfield Park, ch. 44, ¶ 2”
faults.why: Paragraph numbers are edition-dependent, and the notes neither quote nor identify the relevant Austen wording. As given, the citations are not readily verifiable and do not demonstrate that the cited passages support the claimed stylistic moves.

faults.quote: “Judgement in abstract nouns: ‘I was, in truth, sensible only of relief’”
faults.why: This description is imprecise. “Relief” is an abstract noun, but the principal move is the formal construction “sensible of,” together with restriction (“only”) and the qualifying phrase “in truth.” Calling it simply “judgement in abstract nouns” does not teach the actual syntactic mechanism being used.

faults.quote: “Austen opens by balancing the social disruption against the private satisfaction in a single period”
faults.why: This is presented as an account of how Austen would restructure the piece, but the rewrite retains the writer’s original event-to-feeling order and simply combines the first two thoughts into one paragraph. The explanation should say that the order was retained, rather than implying a distinctive reordering.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the central emotional arc and gives it a mostly convincing Austen-like cadence, with the final dry private verdict especially effective. Its main weaknesses are the invented “excuse,” the narrowed sense of “mortification,” and notes whose vague, edition-specific citations do not adequately substantiate or teach the claimed moves.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
And it came to pass at midnight, that Ryan sent unto me a message, and said, We must needs talk together; and straightway I knew what it meant.

And on the morrow we met at a coffee store downtown: and, lo, he was there already, looking upon his phone; and his countenance was troubled. And he said unto me, I am not ready for an earnest thing; and again he said, It is not of thee, but of me.

And my heart sought to weep, but I wept not; and I bowed the head, and said, It is well. Then I walked unto my house in the rain, and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

And my roommate thought that I was moved beyond measure: and peradventure so I was; yet was there grief in my heart.

lessons: Your passage tells a modern grief in tiny, detached statements; the King James manner binds events with “and”, unfolds feelings through bodily signs, and balances thoughts across colons and semicolons. Notice how “And it came to pass at midnight, that Ryan sent unto me a message” sets a measured cadence, and how naming modern things plainly (“a coffee shop”, “ice cream”) lets scripture’s syntax carry contemporary life without turning it into a riddle. outline.gist: Midnight message and foreboding
Meeting at the coffee shop and the breakup words
Silent reaction, walk in rain, and ice cream
Roommate's judgment and lingering hurt

plan.gist: Midnight summons and silent recognition
plan.why: Open with 'And it came to pass at midnight' to establish narrative weight and join the notification with the narrator's immediate dread.
Bring the meeting forward with 'And on the morrow', note his nervous posture plainly, and set his excuses in direct parallel speech.
plan.gist: The encounter at the coffee shop and his rejection

plan.why: Turn emotional restraint into physical signs ('bowed the head', 'It is well') and recount the journey home in polysyndeton.
plan.gist: Restrained grief and retreat into rain and food
External verdict versus internal pain
plan.why: Conclude with the roommate's dismissal balanced against the narrator's unfeigned hurt.

sense.problem: No fault of sense: no contradiction, no person or time left unclear in a way that blocks the reader, no missing step. The timeline (midnight text, next day, walk home) and the speakers (Ryan, the narrator, the roommate) all agree.
sense.resolution: None to mend. The passage is a break-up narrative in a modern idiom; its nearest true echo is the prodigal son's feast-and-squandering aftermath only in the loosest sense, and in fact it is not an echo of that scene at all — there is no departure, return or welcome here. The scene it does faintly resemble is the friend who stays, Ruth 1 ('whither thou goest, I will go'), but the passage contains no such vow and no such person, so there is no true echo and none is claimed.

faults.quote: looking upon his phone
faults.why: This drops the specific action that he was “scrolling” on his phone. Looking at a phone is broader and loses a concrete detail of the original scene.

faults.quote: I am not ready for an earnest thing
faults.why: “An earnest thing” is substantially less clear than “something serious,” and does not naturally preserve the implied serious relationship. It turns a familiar breakup formulation into a vague abstraction.

faults.quote: And my heart sought to weep
faults.why: The original says the narrator wanted to cry but did not. A heart that “sought to weep” changes both the agent and the action, suggesting an inward impulse or attempted weeping rather than the narrator’s consciously restrained desire.

faults.quote: I bowed the head, and said, It is well
faults.why: A nod and “okay” are replaced with a bowed head and the stronger, more composed declaration “It is well.” The latter can imply genuine acceptance or reassurance, whereas the original is spare and potentially resigned.

faults.quote: a coffee store downtown
faults.why: “Coffee store” is not idiomatic English in either modern usage or the King James Bible’s idiom. The biblical register can frame a modern object, but this substitution sounds like costume-archaic diction rather than a natural scriptural phrasing.

faults.quote: an earnest thing
faults.why: This is not a characteristic King James biblical collocation. “Earnest” exists in the translation, but not in this vague nominal construction, which reads as an awkward attempt at antiquity.

faults.quote: And my heart sought to weep
faults.why: The phrasing is intelligible but unidiomatic. Hearts may be sorrowful, faint, or troubled in the King James Bible; “sought to weep” produces an awkward and slightly comic personification.

faults.quote: I am not ready for an earnest thing
faults.why: The phrase is a riddle: the reader has to infer that “thing” means a serious romantic relationship. Its vagueness is not purposeful biblical compression.

faults.quote: And it came to pass ... — cites 1 Thessalonians 3:4
faults.why: 1 Thessalonians 3:4 does not contain “And it came to pass” and is not an apt source for this narrative formula. The citation is inaccurate.

faults.quote: Behold, lo, verily
faults.why: The quoted rewrite uses only “lo”; it contains neither “behold” nor “verily.” The note claims moves that were not made.

faults.quote: and, lo, he was there already, looking upon his phone; and his countenance was troubled. — cites Genesis 15:12
faults.why: Genesis 15:12 contains “lo” but does not support the quoted construction of a troubled countenance or someone looking at an object. It is at best a very loose citation and does not accurately document the stated move.

faults.quote: Parallelism ... — cites Ruth 1:9
faults.why: Ruth 1:9 is not an apt source for the particular claimed parallelism of restrained weeping, bowed head, and “It is well.” The note supplies a citation without showing a real verbal or syntactic model.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore
faults.why: The quoted sentence uses “unto” only; it contains neither “thereof” nor “wherefore.” As with the earlier heading, the note inaccurately lists unused devices.

faults.quote: Then I walked unto my house in the rain, and ate a whole pint of ice cream. — cites Amos 4:7
faults.why: Amos 4:7 does not provide a relevant source for this syntax or vocabulary. Its rain imagery does not justify a citation for the sentence’s use of “unto.”

faults.quote: Clauses laid side by side with “and” ... — cites Genesis 18:32
faults.why: Genesis 18:32 may support “peradventure,” but it is not a fitting source for the note’s stated lesson about clauses joined by “and.” The citation and the described move do not match.

faults.quote: naming modern things plainly (“a coffee shop”, “ice cream”)
faults.why: The rewrite does not say “a coffee shop”; it says “a coffee store.” The lesson inaccurately describes the rewrite and overlooks its least natural modernization.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the overall sequence and much of the emotional movement, and its broad biblical cadence is recognizable. However, it loses some concrete meaning, contains awkward pseudo-biblical wording, and is seriously undermined by inaccurate or mismatched source notes.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
Now it came to pass at the end of the week, that a new family came to dwell in the house next unto our own: and, behold, they had a great truck, and two little children with them. And the father was a pleasant man, and of a good countenance: but his sister, whom we took for their mother, was proud, and stood afar off.

And straightway my mother arose, and baked cakes for them; for she was minded to search out all things concerning them: and she sought to know whence they were come, and what was their occupation, and whether they went to church.

And it was told us that the father was a lawyer, and was unmarried; or rather, that he was divorced from his wife. Then was the countenance of my mother changed, and I knew straightway what was in her heart: for these many years she had sought to give me in marriage.

lessons: The chief difference lies in the cadence of the sentences and the concrete naming of inner feelings. Where your draft relies on casual modern abbreviations and colloquial impressions (“kind of standoffish”, “got this look on her face”), the King James Bible joins clauses with “and” and “for”, expressing emotion through physical tokens such as “stood afar off” and “the countenance of my mother was changed”. Practise building balanced clauses divided by colons and semicolons, letting external signs carry the weight of human motives.

first impressions of the pleasant father and aloof woman
the mother prepares food to discover their history
news arrives that the father is an unmarried lawyer
the mother's calculating reaction and the narrator's dread

plan.why: The voice opens the chronicle with the time and circumstance, introducing the newcomers and their goods.
plan.gist: arrival of the new household next door

plan.why: Scriptural narrative sets contrasting spirits side by side to establish character immediately.
plan.gist: contrasting the pleasant father with the aloof sister

plan.why: Scripture connects hospitality directly with inquiry into lineage and occupation.
plan.gist: the mother's neighbourly gift and desire to investigate

plan.why: The voice states civil station and marital condition plainly, without modern conversational qualifiers.
plan.gist: reporting the man's calling and single estate

plan.why: Grave recognition is conveyed through outward tokens of the visage and the thought of the heart.
plan.gist: the mother's changed countenance and inward intent

faults.quote: “but his sister, whom we took for their mother”
faults.why: The necessary repair requires the aloof woman not to be the divorced man’s wife, but making her specifically his sister, and adding that the narrator mistook her for the children’s mother, invents relationship and backstory not present in the draft. A less invasive repair could retain an unidentified woman in the household.

faults.quote: “was proud, and stood afar off”
faults.why: “Kind of standoffish” conveys social reserve, mildly and tentatively. “Proud” is a much harsher moral judgment in biblical diction, while “stood afar off” primarily describes physical distance. Together they materially intensify and alter the original impression.

faults.quote: “and of a good countenance”
faults.why: A “good countenance” chiefly concerns a person’s face or appearance; it does not reliably mean that he “seems nice.” The rewrite substitutes a visual description for the narrator’s judgment of his character.

faults.quote: “she had sought to give me in marriage”
faults.why: This makes the mother’s intention a formal arrangement of marriage. “Trying to set me up” may mean arranging dates or introductions and carries a lighter, comic degree of pressure; the rewrite strengthens the commitment and certainty of the intention.

faults.quote: “his sister, whom we took for their mother”
faults.why: The pronoun “their” is unclear: it might refer to the children, the newcomers collectively, or the father and sister. The intended repair is inferable, but the sentence should identify her plainly as the children’s presumed mother.

faults.quote: “they had a great truck”
faults.why: “Great” can mean large, but in King James usage it also strongly suggests importance, power, or magnitude. Applied directly to a modern “truck,” it sounds like a modern object supplied with a thin biblical adjective rather than fully natural biblical narrative.

faults.quote: “was unmarried; or rather, that he was divorced from his wife”
faults.why: The correction is logically awkward: a divorced man is ordinarily unmarried. The draft’s “single. Well, divorced” corrects the implication that he had never been married; “or rather” does not clearly express that distinction.

faults.quote: “Behold, lo, verily: ‘and, behold, they had a great truck, and two little children with them.’ — cites James 3:5”
faults.why: The rewrite uses only “behold,” not “lo” or “verily,” and James 3:5 is merely an instance of “Behold,” not a meaningful source for this construction. The note overstates both the move being demonstrated and the relevance of its citation.

faults.quote: “I made the standoffish woman his sister”
faults.why: The note accurately reports the repair, but does not acknowledge that “sister” and the mistaken-mother premise are inventions rather than necessities of the repair. Since the stated standard permits only a mending of the sense fault, that additional liberty should be flagged explicitly as avoidable.

faults.quote: “Scripture connects hospitality directly with inquiry into lineage and occupation.”
faults.why: This structural explanation is asserted without a source and is too broad to be dependable. Biblical hospitality and genealogical inquiry occur, but the claimed direct, standard sequence is not established by the cited passages or by the rewrite.

faults.quote: “the King James Bible joins clauses with ‘and’ and ‘for’”
faults.why: This is useful but incomplete as instruction: it risks teaching that biblical voice is chiefly a matter of sprinkling conjunctions. The lesson does not explain how to preserve the original degree of judgment—for example, why “standoffish” should not become “proud”—or how to make a minimal sense repair without inventing relationships.

judge.verdict: The piece has a recognizable biblical cadence and preserves the original story’s broad sequence, but it overstates the aloof woman’s character and adds unnecessary family history. Its notes identify the central contradiction, yet several source and structural claims are superficial or insufficiently precise.

Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam

Sam unto the team, greeting.

Behold, I write unto you: for the launch is removed from the third day unto the fifth day. For the men of law have not yet set their hand to the pricing page, and I will not that we send it forth without it.

Wherefore let each of you make an end of his part in the deck by Wednesday at noon; and if any of you be hindered, tell me this day, and not on the morrow.

The salutation of me Sam with mine own hand.

lessons: The chief difference lies in the weight of the clauses and the direct epistolary cadence: the Authorized Version turns an informal office memo into an epistle, opening with formal salutation, joining clauses with “and”, and addressing the company plural as “ye”. Practise setting aside modern compressed bullet-points for balanced coordinating clauses, as in “and let your parts of the deck be finished by Wednesday at noon: and if any man be hindered, let him tell me today, and not on the morrow.” This gives gravity and clarity to instructions without adding any foreign piety.

faults.quote: “the launch is removed from the third day unto the fifth day”
faults.why: This does not preserve the stated weekdays, Tuesday and Thursday. In KJV usage, “the third day” and “the fifth day” ordinarily suggest ordinal days or dates, not named weekdays; the original's specific scheduling information is lost.

faults.quote: “The men of law”
faults.why: “Legal” need not consist of men. The rewrite unnecessarily adds a gendered description of people that the writer did not supply.

faults.quote: “Thanks,”
faults.why: The writer's expression of thanks is omitted entirely. “The salutation of me Sam with mine own hand” supplies a signature but not the same courteous feeling.

faults.quote: “from the third day unto the fifth day”
faults.why: It is unclear whether these mean calendar dates, days after an unstated event, or substitutes for weekdays. The original deadline change is clear; this version makes it less so.

faults.quote: “Sam unto the team, greeting.”
faults.why: This imitates the surface shape of an epistolary superscription, but it is not an especially natural Authorized Version formulation. Biblical epistles normally identify the sender with an office or relation and address a defined recipient body; “Sam unto the team” reads as a modern email header with “unto” inserted.

faults.quote: “the men of law have not yet set their hand to the pricing page”
faults.why: “Men of law” is not the Authorized Version's usual designation; it uses terms such as “lawyers” or “doctors of the law.” Moreover, setting one's hand to a page more naturally suggests writing or working on it than formally approving it.

faults.quote: “Unto, thereof, wherefore: ‘Sam unto the team, greeting.’ — cites Deuteronomy 1:42”
faults.why: The quoted sentence contains “unto” but neither “thereof” nor “wherefore.” Deuteronomy 1:42 is not an apt source for this epistolary greeting formula.

faults.quote: “Behold, lo, verily: ‘Behold, I write unto you...’ — cites Genesis 8:13”
faults.why: The rewrite uses only “Behold,” not “lo” or “verily,” and Genesis 8:13 does not support the claimed epistolary move. The citation is inaccurate and does not teach the source of the phrasing.

faults.quote: “Wherefore let each of you... — cites 1 Samuel 20:5”
faults.why: 1 Samuel 20:5 contains coordination with “and,” but it is not a particularly apt source for the imperative construction, the deadline, or the hindrance clause identified in the note. The note overstates what the citation demonstrates.

faults.quote: “The salutation of me Sam with mine own hand.” — cites 1 Corinthians 16:21
faults.why: This is the one very close source, but the notes do not report the substantive fidelity changes: replacing Tuesday and Thursday with ordinal days, introducing “men,” and omitting “Thanks.”

faults.quote: “addressing the company plural as ‘ye’”
faults.why: The rewrite never uses “ye.” The lesson attributes a technique to the rewrite that is absent, reducing its reliability as instruction.

faults.quote: “and let your parts of the deck be finished by Wednesday at noon”
faults.why: The lesson's model sentence is useful in isolation, but it does not explain the important choice between “ye” as subject and “you” as object, nor does it address how to preserve modern fixed facts such as weekday names without turning them into ambiguous biblical ordinals.

faults.quote: “The salutation of me Sam with mine own hand.”
faults.why: As a biblical epistle closing this is recognizable, but for the stated work-email form it displaces the writer's actual thanks rather than adapting both the courtesy close and signature.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the overall sequence and both operational requests, but it loses specific weekday information and the writer's thanks. Its KJV effect is competent at the level of formulas, while the source notes are often inaccurate and the teaching commentary overclaims what the rewrite actually does.

Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Now it is meet that our town shut Main Street unto cars at the end of the week; and behold, the way should be closed against them. For the setting of cars in the midst of the town is a grievous vexation; and the paths, which are by the way, are strait, and too narrow for strollers. And other towns have done after this manner: and behold, their booths do prosper, and they are in better case now, than ever they were heretofore.

And some among the merchants will complain, saying, The buyers cannot come unto us: howbeit, they will become accustomed unto it. For of a truth, the more part of the people walk on foot from the garage notwithstanding.

Wherefore, let us prove this thing in the summer, and make trial thereof.

faults.why: “Them” grammatically refers to “cars,” but cars cannot naturally be the party against whom a way is closed. The antecedent and logic are awkward; the intended meaning is that cars should be excluded from Main Street.

faults.quote: their booths do prosper
faults.why: “Booths” are temporary stalls or shelters, not generally permanent downtown shops. This narrows and alters the writer’s claim about shops.

faults.quote: the paths, which are by the way
faults.why: This is redundant and obscure. Sidewalks are not naturally described as “paths, which are by the way,” and the phrase does not sound like an idiomatic Authorized Version construction.

faults.quote: they will become accustomed unto it
faults.why: The phrase is stiff in a way that is not convincingly biblical. The Authorized Version more naturally uses forms such as “accustom themselves,” where appropriate, rather than “become accustomed unto.”

faults.quote: walk on foot from the garage notwithstanding
faults.why: “Notwithstanding” is stranded at the end without a clear object: notwithstanding what? Although it is meant to convey “anyway,” it produces a syntactic riddle rather than a grave biblical emphasis.

faults.quote: Now it is meet that our town shut Main Street unto cars
faults.why: “Meet” is appropriately biblical, but “shut Main Street unto cars” is not an idiomatic King James formulation. “Unto” is used as a costume replacement for a modern preposition rather than according to its normal biblical syntactic function.

faults.quote: For the setting of cars in the midst of the town
faults.why: This does not convincingly render “parking downtown.” “Setting of cars” sounds invented rather than drawn from Authorized Version diction, and it makes the practical civic point less immediate.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “Now it is meet ...” — cites Jeremiah 39:15
faults.why: Jeremiah 39:15 does not substantiate the stated cluster of diction or this sentence’s construction. It contains “unto Jeremiah,” but it is not an apt source for “meet,” “wherefore,” or the proposed civic formulation.

faults.quote: Behold, lo, verily: “And other towns ...” — cites Matthew 12:41
faults.why: The quoted rewrite does not contain “lo” or “verily,” and Matthew 12:41 is not a meaningful source for the claim that other towns’ shops prosper. The note overstates and misdescribes its own evidence.

faults.quote: The genitive with “of” ... — cites 2 Kings 6:1
faults.why: The note identifies no distinctive, relevant genitive construction and gives a citation that does not explain the rewrite’s phrasing. It is terminology without a usable stylistic lesson.

faults.quote: Paragraph 2: (no notes) / Paragraph 3: (no notes)
faults.why: The second and third paragraphs contain major stylistic changes—merchant dialogue, “of a truth,” the misplaced “notwithstanding,” and “prove this thing”—but the notes neither identify their models nor explain the choices.

faults.quote: Practise joining your rapid claims with biblical conjunctions and prepositions
faults.why: This is too broad and risks teaching decorative archaism rather than transferable rhetorical control. It gives no concrete guidance on when coordination clarifies an argument, how to preserve modern meaning, or how to avoid strained substitutions such as “unto cars.”

judge.verdict: The rewrite retains the argument’s overall sequence and most of its content, but several substitutions distort practical meaning or create awkward syntax. Its surface biblical diction is recognizable, yet the source notes are largely unreliable and do not adequately teach the craft moves they claim to document.

I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I think that we should change our work unto a week of four days: for the people are weary and faint, and our best engineer hath even now departed from us. Moreover there be writings shewing that our work abideth the same, yea, or increaseth; and it would be an help unto us also when we seek to hire men.

I know indeed that it is dangerous, and that our clients may take no pleasure in it: yet might we prove it for the space of three months, and see.

Moreover there be writings shewing that our work abideth the same, yea, or increaseth; and it would be an help unto us also when we seek to hire men.

abideth the same, yea, or increaseth

rows.text: I know indeed that it is dangerous, and that our clients may take no pleasure in it: yet might we prove it for the space of three months, and see.

notes.after: for the space of three months

lessons: The chief difference lies in how thoughts are sustained: your draft moves in brisk, modern declarations, whereas the King James Bible joins its reasons with colons and copulas into a single flowing cadence. Notice how abstract workplace terms like “burned out” and “productivity” gain gravity when turned into plain bodily states and biblical verbs (“weary and faint”, “our work abideth the same, yea, or increaseth”). Practise linking cause and consequence across a colon or semicolon rather than breaking every thought into a fresh sentence.

Reasons: burnout and loss of staff
Evidence of productivity
Additional benefit for hiring

Evidence of work and benefit in hiring
plan.why: Set the outward proofs together, balancing the preservation of labour with the gain in taking men.

plan.gist: Objection weighed and trial proposed
plan.why: Acknowledge the peril and immediately answer it with a measured time of testing.

faults.quote: our work abideth the same, yea, or increaseth
faults.why: This weakens and slightly changes “productivity stays the same or goes up.” Productivity is a measure of output relative to input; “our work” can mean the total work being done, and so does not preserve the original claim with the same precision.

faults.quote: our best engineer hath even now departed from us
faults.why: “Just quit” specifically says that the engineer resigned. “Departed from us” is less definite and can merely mean left, while “even now” can mean at this very moment rather than recently.

faults.quote: change our work unto a week of four days
faults.why: This is biblicizing by substitution rather than idiomatic King James syntax. One may come “unto” a person, place, or object, but “change our work unto a week” is an awkward construction not natural to the KJV.

faults.quote: change our work unto a week of four days
faults.why: The phrase is grammatically and idiomatically strained: one changes a work schedule, or changes work to four days, but does not naturally “change work unto a week.”

faults.quote: There be writings shewing that our work abideth the same
faults.why: “Writings” is too vague for the evidentiary force of “studies,” and “our work abideth” leaves unclear whether the claim concerns output, efficiency, workload, or productivity.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “unto a week of four days”
faults.why: The note claims “thereof” and “wherefore” as moves, but neither word appears in the rewrite. It therefore does not accurately describe the revision.

faults.quote: cites Haggai 2:20
faults.why: Haggai 2:20 contains an ordinary instance of “unto,” but it does not make the particular construction “change our work unto a week” idiomatic or apt. The citation is too thin to support the stated stylistic move.

faults.quote: Parallelism: “abideth the same, yea, or increaseth” — cites Ecclesiastes 1:18
faults.why: Ecclesiastes 1:18 does not furnish this pattern or support this claim: its relevant movement is that increased wisdom brings increased grief and sorrow. It is not an apt source for a balanced same-or-increases productivity formulation.

faults.quote: Paragraph 1
faults.why: The notes do not acknowledge the consequential recasting of “productivity” as “our work,” even though that alteration reduces precision and creates a small sense problem.

faults.quote: abstract workplace terms like “burned out” and “productivity” gain gravity when turned into plain bodily states and biblical verbs
faults.why: The advice usefully identifies a move, but it presents the replacement of “productivity” with “our work abideth” as uncomplicated improvement without warning that technical terms sometimes carry necessary precision. In this instance, the substitution partly changes the argument.

judge.verdict: The rewrite retains the argument and its effective overall order, and several cadential choices are recognizably biblical. But its central scheduling phrase is unnatural, its productivity claim is less precise, and the source notes contain inaccurate and poorly matched citations.

And I said unto her, It is well, and we will do it at another time; howbeit I think not that we shall.

lessons: Where your draft was clipped and modern, the Authorized Version builds its thought through cadence and parallel clauses joined by “and”. It uses concrete signs of feeling (“my heart was not troubled”, “yea, verily I was relieved”) rather than psychological shorthand, and frames direct speech plainly with “said unto her”. Practise giving speech and verdicts room to breathe by balancing your sentences with colons and semicolons.

polite reply and silent disbelief

faults.quote: when Dana put off our dinner
faults.why: “Put off” specifically means postpone, whereas “cancelled” leaves open whether the dinner was merely deferred or abandoned. The following polite promise to do it another time is the speaker's response, not proof that Dana herself postponed it.

faults.quote: Behold, lo, verily: “Yea, verily I was relieved;” — cites John 10:7
faults.why: John 10:7 supplies “Verily, verily,” but not “Yea, verily,” and neither “behold” nor “lo” appears in the rewritten sentence. The note overstates the source's support for the actual wording.

faults.quote: Unto, thereof, wherefore: “and thereof am I not proud.” — cites Psalms 138:6
faults.why: The quoted rewrite contains neither “unto” nor “wherefore,” and Psalm 138:6 does not supply the claimed cluster of diction. This is not an apt or accurate citation for the stated move.

faults.quote: It uses concrete signs of feeling (“my heart was not troubled”, “yea, verily I was relieved”) rather than psychological shorthand
faults.why: “My heart was not troubled” is a more concrete biblical formulation, but “I was relieved” remains a direct abstract statement of feeling. The lesson therefore misdescribes one of its own examples and gives the writer an unreliable distinction.

judge.verdict: The rewrite is clear, structurally faithful, and generally convincing in an Authorized Version register. Its only material textual drift is making the cancellation definitively a postponement, while two source notes are inaccurate.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan sent me a message at midnight, saying we needed to talk, and I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a shop downtown, where he was already sitting with his eyes fixed on his phone. He looked nervous, explaining that he was not ready for something serious—as if any of us ever really feels ready when something matters. He offered the old line, telling me it was not because of me, but because of him.

I wanted to cry, but I held it together, agreed quietly, and said okay. Then I walked back home in the pouring rain, sat down, and took down every last spoon of ice cream in the carton.

My roommate thought I was making too much of the whole thing, and maybe I was. Even so, it still hurt.

lessons: I expanded the clipped sentences into measured, conversational cadences that balance quiet feeling with reflective poise. By setting his nervous excuses against genuine hurt—using balanced antithesis and an appeal to shared human experience—the telling moves from a painful personal moment to an honest recognition of how rejection feels.

outline.gist: Midnight message signaling an ending
Meeting downtown and his nervous breakup excuses
Holding back tears, going home in the rain, and comfort food
Roommate's dismissal versus the lingering sting

plan.why: Join the quick opening lines into a rolling introductory sentence that establishes the narrative arc.
plan.gist: The late-night text and immediate sense of dread
The awkward downtown meeting and well-worn excuses
plan.why: Capture his nervous evasion through balanced clauses and antithesis, allowing the universal truth of the situation to shine through.

plan.gist: Suppressing tears and seeking comfort at home
plan.why: Render the silent heartbreak and lonely retreat in concrete, understated details.

plan.gist: Outside perspective versus personal truth
plan.why: Conclude on a reflective cadence, pairing a concession with a firm, simple acknowledgement of pain.

faults.quote: “at a shop downtown”
faults.why: This drops the specific fact that the meeting took place at a coffee shop. A generic shop is not equivalent to the writer’s stated setting.

faults.quote: “with his eyes fixed on his phone”
faults.why: This replaces the concrete action “scrolling on his phone” with a static image. It preserves that he was looking at a phone, but loses a stated detail.

faults.quote: “as if any of us ever really feels ready when something matters”
faults.why: This adds a broad claim that the relationship, or Ryan’s decision, was about something that “matters.” It is an intrusive elevation of a deliberately plain breakup scene, rather than necessary commentary on an existing fact.

faults.quote: “in the pouring rain”
faults.why: “Pouring” materially intensifies the weather. The original says only that the narrator walked in the rain.

faults.quote: “took down every last spoon of ice cream in the carton”
faults.why: This changes “a whole pint of ice cream” into an unspecified carton and loses the exact quantity. It also adds the idea of eating every last spoonful, which is not quite the same fact.

faults.quote: “as if any of us ever really feels ready when something matters”
faults.why: This is a generic inspirational aphorism, not a persuasive imitation of Obama’s voice. It gestures toward his public rhetoric but lacks his characteristic specificity, measured qualification, and civic or moral argumentative development.

faults.quote: “I held it together, agreed quietly”
faults.why: The phrasing is smooth contemporary memoir prose, but it does not establish a distinctive Obama cadence. Most of the rewrite is merely more polished than the source rather than recognizably modeled on his actual prose.

faults.quote: “took down every last spoon of ice cream in the carton”
faults.why: “Took down” combined with “every last spoon” is awkward for this intimate, sad scene; one normally eats spoonfuls rather than spoons. The phrasing risks sounding performative or unintentionally comic.

faults.quote: “Not this, but that: ‘telling me it was not because of me, but because of him.’ — cites Weekly Address, 7 January 2017, ¶ 2”
faults.why: The note does not show how the cited address specifically supports this move, and the cited wording is principally the writer’s existing breakup cliché recast into formal diction. A generic contrast is not enough to establish a useful or well-supported Obama source connection.

faults.quote: “[liberty] Liberty taken: A characteristic Obama reflection extending one person’s private experience into a universal truth.”
faults.why: The note correctly admits an addition, but it does not acknowledge that the added universal truth also raises the stakes of the scene by calling the relationship something that “matters.” It should explain that tonal consequence and why it is warranted.

faults.quote: “using balanced antithesis and an appeal to shared human experience”
faults.why: The lesson names techniques abstractly but does not teach their mechanics from this passage. It should identify the exact pattern—personal observation, limited generalization, return to concrete action—and explain when a writer should avoid such a generalization so as not to overstate a small scene.

faults.quote: “Capture his nervous evasion through balanced clauses and antithesis”
faults.why: The structural explanation overclaims: the rewrite largely preserves the original scene order and has not developed a substantial balanced-clause structure. The writer is not given a concrete, reusable revision method beyond the vague instruction to make sentences more measured.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the broad narrative and its effective four-part progression, but it loses several concrete facts and substitutes generic elevated prose for a convincing Obama voice. Its notes and lesson identify broad rhetorical labels without sufficiently grounding them in either a reliable source connection or a transferable revision method.

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
Last weekend, a new family moved in next door, pulling up with a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems like a nice man, but his sister lives with them, and she tends to keep to herself.

Right away, my mother made them a warm home of food. She wanted to find out everything she could about them—where they’d come from, what they did for work, and whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer, and he’s not married, but separated. The moment she heard that, my mom got this look on her face, and I knew right away what she was thinking. That’s why she looked at me that way—she’s been trying to set me up for years.

rows.text: Last weekend, a new family moved in next door, pulling up with a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems like a nice man, but his sister lives with them, and she tends to keep to herself.

notes.text: Your first paragraph gives the new family a 'mom'; your third says the dad is single, and the last line aims him at the narrator. I made the standoffish woman the dad's sister who lives with them, so the household can hold an adult woman and a single father at once without clashing with his being separated or with your mother's matchmaking.
notes.after: The dad seems like a nice man, but his sister lives with them, and she tends to keep to herself.

rows.text: Right away, my mother made them a warm home of food. She wanted to find out everything she could about them—where they’d come from, what they did for work, and whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer, and he’s not married, but separated. The moment she heard that, my mom got this look on her face, and I knew right away what she was thinking. That’s why she looked at me that way—she’s been trying to set me up for years.

notes.after: It turns out the dad is a lawyer, and he’s not married, but separated.
