notes.after: That’s why she looked at me that way

lessons: Your draft relied on choppy fragments, whereas President Obama builds conversational momentum through balanced clauses and rhythmic cadences. Notice how grouping your mother’s inquiries into a rhythmic series of three (“where they’d come from, what they did for work, and whether they went to church”) gives her curiosity an affectionate, orderly sweep. Turning the neighbor’s marital status through an antithesis (“not married, but separated”) and pivoting to the ending with a purposeful turn (“That’s why she looked at me that way”) delivers the humorous punchline with measured warmth.

outline.gist: A new family moves in next door with a huge truck, two kids, a nice dad, and a standoffish mom.
The narrator's mother bakes them cookies immediately to learn everything about them.
The dad is revealed to be a divorced lawyer, prompting a matchmaking look from the mother.

plan.why: Establish the scene in balanced, measured narrative clauses while resolving the domestic contradiction early.
plan.gist: Introduce the new neighbors and their household, establishing the friendly father and his reserved sister.
Describe the mother bringing over food to learn who the new neighbors are.
plan.why: Build the mother's curiosity through a parallel cadence of three questions.

plan.gist: Reveal the father's marital status and land on the mother's matchmaking glance.
plan.why: Use an antithesis ('not married, but separated') and close on a purposeful turn to deliver the humor.

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the new family a 'mom'; your third says the dad is single, and the last line aims him at the narrator. A mother and a single (divorced) father cannot both be true of the same household unless the 'mom' is not the dad's partner.
sense.quote: The mom is kind of standoffish. … It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.
sense.resolution: Make her the dad's sister — or another relative living with them — so the house can hold a 'mom'-like figure and a single dad at once: 'The dad's sister lives with them; she's kind of standoffish.' This keeps every other sentence true (two kids, a divorced lawyer father, the mother's matchmaking) and keeps the neighbor's household intact; calling her his ex-wife would clash with divorced-and-single and with her living in his house.

faults.quote: “my mother made them a warm home of food”
faults.why: This drops the specific action that she “baked them cookies” and replaces it with a different, vaguer act. The cookies are a concrete comic detail and should have been retained.

faults.quote: “he’s not married, but separated”
faults.why: The source says the father is “single. Well, divorced.” Separation is not divorce and can imply an ongoing marriage. This changes a central fact rather than repairing the actual contradiction.

faults.quote: “That’s why she looked at me that way”
faults.why: The writer says the mother “got this look on her face”; it does not say she looked at the narrator. The rewrite invents the direction of her glance.

faults.quote: “pulling up with a huge truck”
faults.why: The draft says the family has a huge truck, not that the narrator saw them arrive in it. This is a small but unnecessary added event.

faults.quote: “he’s not married, but separated”
faults.why: The stated sense repair should resolve the apparent presence of a mother with a divorced, single father. Recasting him as separated does not do so cleanly: a separated person may still be married, and it contradicts the draft’s explicit correction, “Well, divorced.”

faults.quote: “made them a warm home of food”
faults.why: This is not idiomatic English. One can make someone feel at home, bring food to a home, or offer a warm welcome, but not ordinarily “make them a warm home of food.”

faults.quote: “That’s why she looked at me that way”
faults.why: The line is awkwardly explanatory and presupposes an established look directed at the narrator that the preceding sentence has not supplied.

faults.quote: “The dad seems like a nice man, but his sister lives with them, and she tends to keep to herself.”
faults.why: The sentence reads as plain contemporary exposition rather than Obama’s characteristic reflective, public-facing, oratory-informed prose. The added domestic clarification is functional but has no distinctive cadence or rhetorical pressure.

faults.quote: “That’s why she looked at me that way—she’s been trying to set me up for years.”
faults.why: The causal restatement is mechanically explicit and conversationally generic. It does not convincingly reproduce a recognizable Obama syntactic move, and the dash is doing work that the sentence’s rhythm does not earn.

faults.quote: “Not this, but that: ‘It turns out the dad is a lawyer, and he’s not married, but separated.’”
faults.why: The note misidentifies the construction as a meaningful Obama-style antithesis and provides no justification for changing “divorced” to “separated.” More importantly, it fails to report this consequential factual alteration as a liberty or sense repair.

faults.quote: “From what happened to what we do: ‘That’s why she looked at me that way—she’s been trying to set me up for years.’”
faults.why: The quoted sentence does not move from an event to a collective response or action; it merely explains the mother’s expression. The named move does not accurately describe the revision, so the citation does not teach a usable technique.

faults.quote: “The voice explicitly connects the mother's expression to her long-standing habit of matchmaking.”
faults.why: That connection was already explicit in the source: the narrator knows what the mother is thinking because she has been trying to set the narrator up for years. The note wrongly presents a source-preserving restatement as a special liberty.

faults.quote: “Your draft relied on choppy fragments”
faults.why: This misdescribes the draft. It consists chiefly of concise complete sentences; only “Well, divorced” is a deliberate fragment. The lesson therefore begins from an inaccurate diagnosis.

faults.quote: “Turning the neighbor’s marital status through an antithesis (‘not married, but separated’)”
faults.why: This recommends a revision that changes the source fact and calls a clarification of marital status an antithesis. It teaches a potentially harmful habit—altering facts for rhetorical symmetry—rather than a transferable structural move.

faults.quote: “As the voice would build it: setting (Introduce the new neighbors and their household, establishing the friendly father and his reserved sister.”
faults.why: The outline normalizes the invented sister and does not flag that the original’s “mom” had to be recast to resolve the contradiction. It should distinguish the necessary sense repair from the writer’s original material.

judge.verdict: The rewrite identifies the real household contradiction and offers a plausible repair, but it unnecessarily changes the father from divorced to separated and loses the cookies. Its Obama imitation is mostly generic polished narration, while several notes and teaching claims misdescribe both the source and the revision.

faults.why: The original has a conventional email closing with “Thanks,” followed by the sender's name. Putting both into one sentence makes the sign-off less natural and visually weaker as an email close.

faults.quote: Liberty taken: The voice frames the new preparation deadline as a direct consequence of the legal delay
faults.why: The note accurately identifies the added causal framing, but treats it as a stylistic liberty rather than flagging that it adds a relationship not stated by the writer. This is not a repair of a fault of sense.

faults.quote: The chief difference is that your draft delivers instructions as clipped updates, whereas President Obama frames an operational shift as a shared responsibility governed by clear standards.
faults.why: The lesson overstates what the rewrite actually does. The rewrite says “I need” and “come tell me,” but does not substantially frame the work as shared responsibility; the claimed lesson is therefore only partly grounded in the revision.

faults.quote: Practise using balanced antithesis (“tell me today -- not tomorrow”) to make your expectations unmistakable.
faults.why: This is a usable technique, but the lesson does not warn that “That is why” creates a causal claim. It therefore teaches a structural move without distinguishing legitimate connective logic from an invented factual relationship.

faults.quote: That is why
faults.why: The original order was already sound for a short operational email. Making the deck deadline an explicit consequence of legal approval slightly distorts that structure rather than merely sharpening the transition.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the central operational facts and retains a workable email form, but it introduces an unsupported causal connection between the legal issue and the deck deadline. Its Obama resemblance is competent but fairly surface-level, and the teaching notes should distinguish stylistic linkage from added meaning.

yours:
Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
When the weekend comes, our town ought to close Main Street to cars. Right now, finding a spot to leave your car downtown is an ordeal, and the walks are simply too narrow for parents pushing young children. Communities nearby have already taken this step, and their local shops are not suffering—they’re doing better than ever.

Now, some business owners will complain that customers cannot reach them. But given time, they’ll adapt to the change. Because the truth is, most folks already walk from where they leave their cars anyway.

That’s why we ought to come together and give this a try this summer.

rows.text: When the weekend comes, our town ought to close Main Street to cars. Right now, finding a spot to leave your car downtown is an ordeal, and the walks are simply too narrow for parents pushing young children. Communities nearby have already taken this step, and their local shops are not suffering—they’re doing better than ever.

notes.text: Echo: the turn from complaint to proposal, relying on outside precedent to justify a local trial, echoes the argument-by-example in the Selma and Tucson addresses. I grounded the claim in what neighboring communities have already achieved, meeting the merchant objection in their own terms before landing on a concrete, low-stakes summer trial.
notes.after: Communities nearby have already taken this step, and their local shops are not suffering—they’re doing better than ever.

rows.text: Now, some business owners will complain that customers cannot reach them. But given time, they’ll adapt to the change. Because the truth is, most folks already walk from where they leave their cars anyway.

notes.after: Because the truth is, most folks already walk from where they leave their cars anyway.
notes.cite: A Memorial Service for the Victims of the Shooting in Tucson, Arizona, 12 January 2011, ¶ 13

rows.text: That’s why we ought to come together and give this a try this summer.

notes.technique: From what happened to what we do
notes.after: That’s why we ought to come together and give this a try this summer.

notes.text: The voice frames a municipal change as a shared civic endeavor rather than a mere administrative regulation.
notes.after: come together

lessons: Your draft laid out a sound civic proposal, but President Obama builds momentum by meeting doubts head-on and turning local mechanics into common purpose. Turn objections with antithesis, showing that nearby shops “are not suffering—they’re doing better than ever”, which reassures hesitant listeners by contrasting anxiety with proven results. Then turn from the evidence to what we do next using thatswhy in “That’s why we ought to come together”, inviting the listener into a shared, practical step forward.

outline.gist: close Main Street to cars on weekends
parking is hard and sidewalks are too narrow
other towns succeeded with this
merchants will worry about customer access
merchants will adjust
people walk from parking anyway
try it this summer

plan.gist: propose opening the street to people on weekends
plan.why: State the goal simply and positively at the start, framing it around the community rhythm.

plan.gist: contrast current congestion with nearby success
plan.why: Lay out the practical difficulties first, then ground the solution in what other towns have already proven.

plan.gist: acknowledge merchant concerns and answer them with daily facts
plan.why: Meet the skeptic fairly in their own terms before showing that people already walk anyway.
Close not with an unyielding mandate, but with an invitation to come together and test it out.
plan.gist: invite the town to try a modest, seasonal trial

sense.problem: No fault of sense: nothing contradicts anything else, no person or time is left unclear in a way that breaks the argument, and no needed step is missing. The passage is short but sound.
sense.quote: Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends.

sense.problem: Echo: the turn from complaint to proposal, the outside example, and the small reversible trial are all in the manner of his movement for ordinary people's rights and the call to try — the towns that did better, and the closing ask, recall the argument-by-example and the invitation to act in the Selma and Tucson speeches.
sense.quote: Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.
sense.resolution: The rewrite may take from Selma the method of grounding a claim in what ordinary people have already done and letting their example carry the ask; and from the whole body of his speeches the habit of meeting the skeptic's objection in the skeptic's own voice before answering it, then ending on a concrete, doable step rather than a demand. It should take nothing from the funeral eulogies, whose grief is not this matter's.

faults.quote: Communities nearby have already taken this step
faults.why: The draft says only that “Other towns” have done this. “Nearby” invents a geographic relationship and makes the precedent more locally relevant than the writer established.

faults.quote: the walks are simply too narrow for parents pushing young children
faults.why: This narrows and alters “sidewalks are too narrow for strollers.” A stroller can be pushed by someone other than a parent, and “the walks” is not the same concrete civic feature as sidewalks.

faults.quote: the walks are simply too narrow
faults.why: “The walks” is an awkward, somewhat non-American substitute for “sidewalks,” rather than Obama’s usual plain civic vocabulary. It reads as a stylistic substitution made for effect, not as his natural idiom.

faults.quote: most folks already walk from where they leave their cars anyway
faults.why: The repetition of the act of parking as “where they leave their cars” is clunky. The original’s “walk from the garage” is cleaner and more concrete; this sentence loses that ease.

faults.quote: [sense] Sense: Echo: the turn from complaint to proposal
faults.why: This is not a sense mending. The draft has no stated contradiction or ambiguity that required repair, and the note does not identify one. It is a stylistic/structural rationale incorrectly labeled as a sense intervention.

faults.quote: the argument-by-example in the Selma and Tucson addresses
faults.why: The note invokes two sources without providing citations for either, unlike the later notes. It also does not identify a particular passage or explain what precise formal move was borrowed beyond the generic use of precedent.

faults.quote: I grounded the claim in what neighboring communities have already achieved
faults.why: The note inaccurately describes the rewrite’s change as grounding the claim in the draft’s evidence. “Neighboring” is an added fact, not an interpretation of “Other towns,” and the note does not disclose it as a liberty.

faults.quote: meeting the merchant objection in their own terms before landing on a concrete, low-stakes summer trial
faults.why: The explanation is structurally inaccurate: the merchant objection is not met in paragraph 1, but in paragraph 2. “Low-stakes” is also an added characterization not present in the draft.

faults.quote: Plain talk to the listener: “Because the truth is, most folks already walk from where they leave their cars anyway.” — cites A Memorial Service for the Victims of the Shooting in Tucson, Arizona, 12 January 2011, ¶ 13
faults.why: The note offers a highly specific citation but does not explain the connection between that memorial address and this mundane parking observation. The cited source is not evidently apt for the claimed move, so the citation feels decorative rather than instructional.

faults.quote: using thatswhy in “That’s why we ought to come together”
faults.why: “thatswhy” is a typo, and the lesson reduces a reusable transition to a catchphrase rather than showing how evidence specifically warrants the proposed trial. It gives some advice, but not enough concrete guidance for adapting the move in the writer’s own voice.

faults.quote: As the voice would build it: claim (propose opening the street to people on weekends
faults.why: “Opening the street to people” is a more affirmative reframing than the writer’s specific proposal to close it to cars. It is a plausible rhetorical gloss, but the structural comparison should flag that framing change rather than present it as the same claim.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the argument’s main sequence and improves its civic cadence, but it adds unsupported local detail and occasionally substitutes awkward phrasing for genuine Obama-like plainness. Its notes overclaim source support, mislabel a stylistic explanation as a sense repair, and do not clearly disclose the added “nearby” premise.

yours:
I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I think it’s fair to say that we ought to switch to working four days a week. Folks are worn down, and our best engineer just decided to quit. The studies show that productivity does not drop, but stays steady or even rises. And making this change would also help us when it comes to hiring.

Now, I know this step is risky, and our clients might not like it at first. That’s why we could try it for three months and see how it works.

rows.text: I think it’s fair to say that we ought to switch to working four days a week. Folks are worn down, and our best engineer just decided to quit. The studies show that productivity does not drop, but stays steady or even rises. And making this change would also help us when it comes to hiring.

notes.after: Folks are worn down, and our best engineer just decided to quit.
The studies show that productivity does not drop, but stays steady or even rises.
notes.cite: State of the Union Address, 20 January 2015, ¶ 3

notes.text: Framing the proposal with “it’s fair to say” establishes Obama’s characteristic reasonable, measured posture before advocating for change.
notes.after: I think it’s fair to say that we ought to switch to working four days a week.

rows.text: Now, I know this step is risky, and our clients might not like it at first. That’s why we could try it for three months and see how it works.

notes.technique: From what happened to what we do
notes.after: That’s why we could try it for three months and see how it works.

notes.text: Opening the trial proposal with “That’s why” frames the temporary pilot as the logical, common-sense answer to both the team’s needs and the client risks.
notes.after: That’s why we could try it for three months and see how it works.

lessons: Where your draft stated the case in blunt, unadorned claims, President Obama builds an argument by pairing human empathy with measured practicality. By recasting the evidence through antithesis—“productivity does not drop, but stays steady or even rises”—and concluding with the purposeful turn “That’s why we could try it for three months,” the rewrite converts a stark proposal into a sensible, shared experiment. Practise framing risks and proposals as natural steps toward a workable compromise rather than bare assertions.

outline.gist: Proposing a four-day workweek.
Team burnout and the departure of the best engineer.
Studies showing productivity is maintained or increased.
Aiding future hiring.
Acknowledging risk and client hesitation.
Suggesting a three-month trial.

plan.why: Open with a reasonable, non-dogmatic assertion that invites dialogue.
plan.gist: State the case for a four-day week in measured terms.

plan.why: Ground the proposal in the lived experience of the workers and a concrete loss.
plan.gist: Acknowledge the strain on the team in human language.

plan.why: Use antithesis to directly address the assumed downside of fewer hours.
plan.gist: Cite evidence by contrasting fear with findings.
Point to the recruiting advantage.
plan.why: Highlight an organizational upside to show the change serves long-term growth.

plan.gist: Acknowledge risk and client skepticism fairly.
plan.why: Show understanding for opposing viewpoints before offering an answer.
Close with 'That’s why' to present the pilot as a pragmatic, low-risk compromise.
plan.gist: Propose a trial as the natural next step.

faults.quote: The studies show that productivity does not drop
faults.why: The draft says only that there are studies showing productivity stays the same or rises. This wording upgrades that limited report into the rewrite's unqualified assertion that the studies establish no drop in productivity.

faults.quote: our best engineer just decided to quit
faults.why: “Just decided to quit” adds a deliberative characterization of the engineer's departure that the draft does not give. The original says the engineer “just quit.”

faults.quote: our clients might not like it at first
faults.why: “At first” invents a temporal qualification: the writer acknowledges possible client dislike, not a prediction that it will fade after an initial period.

faults.quote: I think it’s fair to say that we ought to switch to working four days a week.
faults.why: This is generically cautious managerial prose. The stacked hedges “I think” and “it’s fair to say,” followed by the bureaucratic “ought to switch to working,” do not produce a notably Obama-like cadence or rhetorical turn.

faults.quote: And making this change would also help us when it comes to hiring.
faults.why: “When it comes to hiring” is generic contemporary business phrasing rather than a distinctive Obama syntactic or rhetorical move; it merely smooths the original without substantially realizing the stated voice.

faults.quote: “Folks are worn down, and our best engineer just decided to quit.” — cites Howard University Commencement Ceremony, 7 May 2016, ¶ 48
faults.why: The note presents a highly specific citation but does not identify a parallel construction or quote from the speech that supports this claimed move. The cited sentence is largely a direct modernization of the writer's content, including the unsupported addition “decided to.”

faults.quote: “The studies show that productivity does not drop, but stays steady or even rises.” — cites State of the Union Address, 20 January 2015, ¶ 3
faults.why: The note calls this “Not this, but that,” but supplies no actual source language demonstrating that this particular evidence-framing pattern comes from the cited passage. More importantly, it does not disclose that the rewrite has strengthened the writer's epistemic claim.

faults.quote: “That’s why we could try it for three months and see how it works.” — cites Weekly Address, 21 September 2013, ¶ 6
faults.why: “That’s why” is too commonplace to establish a voice-specific borrowing by itself. The note also fails to report the added “how it works,” which subtly narrows the original open-ended “see” into an implementation evaluation.

faults.quote: President Obama builds an argument by pairing human empathy with measured practicality.
faults.why: The lesson is directionally useful but too broad to teach much beyond this short example. It does not distinguish which of the proposed changes are safe stylistic moves and which alter the writer's degree of certainty or add unstated implications.

faults.quote: Where your draft stated the case in blunt, unadorned claims
faults.why: This characterization needlessly diminishes the writer's effective concise structure. The writer already includes claim, concrete organizational harm, evidence, benefit, objection, and a low-risk pilot; the lesson should teach how to develop that structure rather than imply it is merely blunt.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the argument's overall order and persuasive structure, but it is only lightly Obama-inflected and introduces small unsupported shifts in certainty and implication. Its source notes are insufficiently substantiated and fail to disclose the meaningful fidelity changes.

yours:
When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana told me she could not make dinner, I was not upset in the least. Now, I’ll be the first to admit that I was relieved. For the entire week I had worried about our plans, and I am not proud of that.

So I told her it was fine, and that we would get together not tonight but another time. And that is why I do not think we ever will.

rows.text: When Dana told me she could not make dinner, I was not upset in the least. Now, I’ll be the first to admit that I was relieved. For the entire week I had worried about our plans, and I am not proud of that.
So I told her it was fine, and that we would get together not tonight but another time. And that is why I do not think we ever will.

notes.after: not tonight but another time

notes.technique: From what happened to what we do
notes.after: And that is why I do not think we ever will.
notes.cite: Worcester Technical High School Commencement Ceremony, 11 June 2014, ¶ 29

notes.text: The voice frames the final realization as an explicit consequence of the unspoken strain and polite evasion, turning a private thought into an earned conclusion.
notes.after: And that is why

lessons: Your draft leaned on abrupt statements and casual phrasing, whereas President Obama achieves intimacy through measured cadence and candid self-scrutiny. Notice how plain conversational framing like “Now, I’ll be the first to admit” invites the listener into your confidence, while balancing the turn with “not tonight but another time” sharpens the polite excuse. Concluding with “And that is why” gives the final sentence the weight of an earned realization rather than a stray thought.

outline.gist: Dana calls off dinner without causing upset
Relief and confession of having dreaded it all week
Polite excuse to meet again
Quiet conviction that they will not meet

plan.why: State the incident plainly without theatrical grievance, grounding the scene in measured honesty.
plan.gist: Acknowledge the broken plans plainly without distress

plan.why: Turn to conversational frankness, confessing a private shortcoming directly to the listener.
plan.gist: Admit relief and the private shame of having worried over it

plan.why: Balance what was said aloud against the reality of the situation using antithesis.
plan.gist: Offer a polite face to the friend
Draw the quiet, inevitable conclusion
plan.why: End on what the moment truly signifies with a measured verdict that lands firmly.

faults.quote: she could not make dinner
faults.why: This subtly changes a cancellation into an inability to attend. Someone may cancel dinner despite being able to make it; the original gives no reason for Dana’s cancellation.

faults.quote: For the entire week I had worried about our plans
faults.why: “Worried about our plans” is not the same feeling as “dreading it.” It softens the speaker’s aversion to the dinner and broadens the object from the dinner itself to unspecified plans.

faults.quote: not tonight but another time
faults.why: “Tonight” is newly supplied. The original says only that Dana cancelled dinner, not when it had been scheduled.

faults.quote: And that is why I do not think we ever will.
faults.why: The original gives a quiet doubt that they will reschedule dinner. “Ever” broadens this toward a prediction that they will never get together at all, while “that is why” invents a definite causal inference that the original does not state.

faults.quote: And that is why I do not think we ever will.
faults.why: The stated reason is unclear. The preceding sentence reports a polite assurance that they will meet another time; it does not itself establish why they will not. The notes supply an alleged “unspoken strain and polite evasion,” but neither is explicit in the writer’s draft.

faults.quote: not tonight but another time
faults.why: The antithesis sounds imposed rather than idiomatic in this intimate situation. “Not tonight” answers a specific temporal expectation that the passage never establishes, making the phrase feel like rhetoric added for its own sake.

faults.quote: And that is why I do not think we ever will.
faults.why: This is a generic, mechanically signposted conclusion rather than a particularly distinctive Obama cadence. The causal framing is more formal than the restrained private realization in the source passage, and it overexplains the turn.

faults.quote: The voice frames the final realization as an explicit consequence of the unspoken strain and polite evasion
faults.why: This liberty note identifies added material but treats it as a permissible vocal framing. “Unspoken strain” and “polite evasion” are interpretations not established by the draft, and the note does not report that the rewrite has broadened the prediction with “ever.”

faults.quote: From what happened to what we do: “And that is why I do not think we ever will.”
faults.why: The description is inaccurate: the sentence does not move to “what we do,” but to the narrator’s prediction. It also fails to explain the actual structural alteration—the addition of a causal conclusion.

faults.quote: Concluding with “And that is why” gives the final sentence the weight of an earned realization rather than a stray thought.
faults.why: This teaches the writer to add an explicit causal connector even when the passage has not supplied a reason. In this text, the original’s understated doubt is a deliberate strength; the lesson should distinguish earned inference from unsupported explanation.

faults.quote: Your draft leaned on abrupt statements and casual phrasing
faults.why: This is too broad and somewhat misleading for a four-sentence intimate vignette. The original’s short, plain statements are appropriate to its restrained confession; the lesson does not identify which compression or sequencing choice the writer could preserve while revising.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the broad emotional direction and order, but it softens “dreading,” adds an unsupported time reference and causality, and strengthens the final prediction. Its teaching materials offer some usable ideas about cadence and contrast, but they endorse additions that the source does not earn.

Ryan texted me at midnight. He said we needed to talk. I knew right away what that meant.

The next day we met at a coffee shop downtown. He was already there, scrolling on his phone. He looked nervous. He said he wasn't ready for something serious. He said it wasn't me, it was him.

I wanted to cry but I didn't. I just nodded and said okay. Then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate thought I was overreacting. Maybe I was. But it still hurt.
rewrite:
Ryan sent me a message at midnight to say we had got to have a talk; and I knew right off what that meant, without any calling for an interpreter.

Next day we met at a coffee-house downtown, where he was already sitting and turning over his telephone, looking nervous enough to jump out of his boots. He said he warn’t ready for anything serious yet; and he made haste to say it wasn’t me, it was him.

I wanted to cry, but I held in and never let on; I only nodded my head and said all right, and then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

My roommate was of the opinion that I was taking on beyond all reason; and maybe I was, but it hurt, all the same.

rows.text: Ryan sent me a message at midnight to say we had got to have a talk; and I knew right off what that meant, without any calling for an interpreter.

Next day we met at a coffee-house downtown, where he was already sitting and turning over his telephone, looking nervous enough to jump out of his boots. He said he warn’t ready for anything serious yet; and he made haste to say it wasn’t me, it was him.
I wanted to cry, but I held in and never let on; I only nodded my head and said all right, and then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

notes.after: I wanted to cry, but I held in and never let on; I only nodded my head and said all right, and then I walked home in the rain and ate a whole pint of ice cream.

rows.text: My roommate was of the opinion that I was taking on beyond all reason; and maybe I was, but it hurt, all the same.

lessons: The rewrite binds the short, disjointed sentences into Twain’s characteristic cumulative rhythms with “and” and semicolons, turning modern jargon into plain nineteenth-century equivalents like “telephone” and “all right.” It replaces deadpan modern understatement with vernacular asides such as “I reckoned” and “without any calling for an interpreter.”

outline.gist: Ryan sends a late message saying they need to talk, and the narrator anticipates bad news.
They meet at a coffee shop where Ryan delivers the breakup speech.
The narrator suppresses tears, leaves in the rain, and eats ice cream.
The roommate judges the narrator's reaction, but the pain remains real.

plan.why: Begin with the late summons and the narrator's immediate foreboding, joined into a balanced sentence.
plan.gist: Late message and immediate dread of what it means.
Meeting at the coffee shop and hearing his excuses.
plan.why: Set the uncomfortable scene at the coffee shop before landing his canned excuses flatly.

plan.gist: Nodding along, walking home in rain, and eating ice cream.
plan.why: Chain the suppression of grief and the subsequent physical retreat into a single cumulative sentence.
End on the roommate's opinion balanced against the flat, unarguable reality of the hurt.
plan.gist: Roommate's assessment versus the enduring sting.

faults.quote: “turning over his telephone”
faults.why: This does not preserve the specific action of “scrolling on his phone”; it suggests physically handling or rotating the telephone instead.

faults.quote: “looking nervous enough to jump out of his boots”
faults.why: The original says only that Ryan looked nervous. This comic extreme intensifies the degree of his nervousness beyond what the writer states.

faults.quote: “he made haste to say it wasn’t me”
faults.why: “Made haste” adds a new implication of eagerness or urgency in Ryan’s delivery that is not present in the draft.

faults.quote: “He said he warn’t ready”
faults.why: The conspicuous dialect spelling is a superficial Twain marker rather than a consistently established narrator’s idiom. It sits uneasily beside the otherwise relatively standard, modern first-person voice.

faults.quote: “coffee-house downtown”
faults.why: This is a light period-costume substitution rather than a strongly Twainian transformation. Twain’s characteristic voice depends more on a stable speaking consciousness, exact comic observation, and controlled vernacular than on scattered old-fashioned terms.

faults.quote: “I wanted to cry, but I held in and never let on”
faults.why: “Held in” is incomplete and unidiomatic here: one holds in tears, breath, or emotion, rather than simply “holds in.”

faults.quote: “turning over his telephone”
faults.why: Besides changing the action, the phrase is unclear and unnatural as a description of someone using a phone. It can mean examining or physically flipping it, not scrolling.

faults.quote: “cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 12, ¶ 6”
faults.why: The note does not establish that the cited passage actually models this sentence’s particular cumulative construction, and the citation is too imprecise to teach the writer what Twain is doing in the source. It gives no quoted source passage or explanation of the syntactic resemblance.

faults.quote: “The rewrite binds the short, disjointed sentences into Twain’s characteristic cumulative rhythms”
faults.why: This is too broad and does not accurately distinguish the original’s deliberately spare emotional pacing from the rewrite’s one expanded sentence. It names a technique but does not explain where to use it, how much to combine, or what emotional effect the combination produces.

faults.quote: “vernacular asides such as ‘I reckoned’”
faults.why: “I reckoned” does not appear anywhere in the rewrite. The lesson therefore inaccurately describes its own revision.

faults.quote: “turning modern jargon into plain nineteenth-century equivalents like ‘telephone’ and ‘all right’”
faults.why: Neither “texted” nor “scrolling” is usefully taught through this claim, and “telephone” is not an instructive nineteenth-century equivalent for a contemporary texting action. The lesson encourages cosmetic antiquing instead of explaining Twain’s usable methods of narration, understatement, and comic qualification.

judge.verdict: The narrative order and emotional arc are preserved cleanly, but the Twain effect is mostly a thin layer of dialect and antique phrasing. The supporting notes are notably weak: the sole source note is not meaningfully explained, and the lesson inaccurately claims the rewrite contains “I reckoned.”

A new family moved in next door last weekend. They have a huge truck and two little kids. The dad seems nice. The mom is kind of standoffish.

My mother baked them cookies right away. She wanted to find out everything about them. Where they came from, what they did for work, whether they went to church.

It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced. My mom got this look on her face. I knew exactly what she was thinking. She has been trying to set me up for years.
rewrite:
A new family moved into the house next door the other day, with a huge great truck of goods and two little children. The father seemed friendly and pleasant enough; but his sister, who had come to keep house for him, was rather offish.

My mother went straight to work and baked them a batch of sweet cakes, being bound to find out everything there was to know about them. She wanted to know where they had come from, and what trade the man followed, and whether they went to church.

It turned out the father was a lawyer, and had no wife—well, divorced, I reckon, but single all the same. Mother took on a certain look in her face the minute she heard it; and I knew just exactly what she was thinking, because she has been trying to get me married off for years.

rows.text: A new family moved into the house next door the other day, with a huge great truck of goods and two little children. The father seemed friendly and pleasant enough; but his sister, who had come to keep house for him, was rather offish.

notes.text: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mom; your third says the dad is single (divorced). Both cannot be true of the same household at the same time, if he is to be an available match. I made the woman his sister who came along to keep house for him, removing the contradiction while keeping a standoffish woman in the house for the mother to encounter.
notes.after: his sister, who had come to keep house for him, was rather offish

rows.text: My mother went straight to work and baked them a batch of sweet cakes, being bound to find out everything there was to know about them. She wanted to know where they had come from, and what trade the man followed, and whether they went to church.

It turned out the father was a lawyer, and had no wife—well, divorced, I reckon, but single all the same. Mother took on a certain look in her face the minute she heard it; and I knew just exactly what she was thinking, because she has been trying to get me married off for years.

notes.after: well, divorced, I reckon

notes.text: The narrator adds a dry vernacular qualification to reconcile the lawyer's divorce with his eligibility for courtship.
notes.after: I reckon, but single all the same

lessons: Your draft tells the facts in short, clipped statements, whereas Twain lets his narrator speak in an easy, rhythmic drawl that strings observations together. Notice how the vernacular turn “My mother went straight to work and baked them a batch of sweet cakes” grounds the domestic scene in living speech, while the casual aside “well, divorced, I reckon” delivers the narrator’s wry judgment without fanfare. By joining inquiries with polysyndeton in “where they had come from, and what trade the man followed, and whether they went to church,” the sentence captures the relentless, rolling curiosity of a small-town neighbor.

outline.gist: A new family moves in next door with two kids, a pleasant father, and an offish sister.
The mother rushes over with baked goods to pry into their background.
The mother discovers the father is single and eyes him as a match for the narrator.

plan.why: Twain gathers the arrivals into a couple of balanced, rolling sentences rather than four staccato lines.
plan.gist: Establish the arrival of the new household and its members.

plan.why: Presents her gossipy investigation through an active vernacular momentum and rhythmic polysyndeton.
plan.gist: The mother's nosy culinary expedition.

plan.why: Builds up to the deadpan turn at the end of the sentence where the narrator sees through the mother's scheming.
plan.gist: The disclosure of eligibility and the mother's matrimonial eye.

sense.problem: Your first paragraph gives the new family a mom; your third says the dad is single (divorced). Both cannot be true of the same household at the same time — a standoffish woman living in the house with the kids is being presented as his wife, then he is presented as unmarried.
sense.quote: The mom is kind of standoffish. ... It turns out the dad is a lawyer and he's single. Well, divorced.
sense.resolution: The least change that removes the fault: make the woman in the first paragraph something other than the dad's wife — call her his sister (or, if you prefer, say the mother of the kids is not in the picture and this is his sister helping out). Then 'single — well, divorced' agrees with every other sentence, and the setup still supplies a woman in the house for the narrator's mother to read as standoffish. Do not mend it by making the dad not single, because the whole point of the last paragraph is that he is available.

faults.quote: "the other day"
faults.why: This weakens the specific timing of "last weekend" rather than preserving it.

faults.quote: "a huge great truck of goods"
faults.why: The draft says the family has a huge truck; it does not say that the truck is laden with goods. This changes the object from a vehicle they own into a conveyance of their moving possessions.

faults.quote: "his sister, who had come to keep house for him"
faults.why: Changing the apparent mother into another woman in the household is a reasonable reported sense mending, but "who had come to keep house for him" is an invented circumstance not needed to resolve the contradiction.

faults.quote: "a batch of sweet cakes"
faults.why: Cookies have been changed into sweet cakes. The alteration is not necessary for clarity or for a Twain-like syntax, and it loses a concrete domestic fact.

faults.quote: "get me married off"
faults.why: Being "set up" can mean being introduced or pushed toward dates; "married off" makes the mother's aim more final and forceful. It modestly changes the degree of the narrator's complaint.

faults.quote: "The father seemed friendly and pleasant enough; but his sister, who had come to keep house for him, was rather offish."
faults.why: The sentence has some period coloring, but its formal family labels, explanatory relative clause, and "rather offish" read more like generalized old-fashioned prose than a distinctly Twainian narrator.

faults.quote: "well, divorced, I reckon, but single all the same"
faults.why: Adding "I reckon" alone does not create Twain's characteristic comic logic or idiomatic narrative voice. The qualification is also mechanically inserted rather than arising naturally from the narrator's perspective.

faults.quote: "a huge great truck of goods"
faults.why: This is awkward and semantically odd. A "truck of goods" suggests a load or delivery rather than the family's conspicuously large vehicle.

faults.quote: "the mother to encounter"
faults.why: The sense note adopts unnecessarily stiff language for an otherwise practical explanation, and it obscures that the original simply describes the woman as standoffish.

faults.quote: "The writer's: setting (A new family moves in next door with two kids, a pleasant father, and an offish sister.)"
faults.why: This inaccurately describes the writer's draft. The draft says "The mom is kind of standoffish," not that there is an offish sister; the sister exists only after the rewrite's sense mending.

faults.quote: "cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 23, ¶ 30"
faults.why: The note does not identify a relevant quoted passage or explain the connection beyond a bare chapter-and-paragraph citation. Paragraph numbers vary by edition, and this is not an adequately verifiable or instructive source attribution for the claimed move.

faults.quote: "Liberty taken: The narrator adds a dry vernacular qualification to reconcile the lawyer's divorce with his eligibility for courtship."
faults.why: This describes a change but does not acknowledge the more consequential invention that the woman is a housekeeping sister, nor explain why that specific solution was chosen over other possible household relationships.

faults.quote: "Your draft tells the facts in short, clipped statements, whereas Twain lets his narrator speak in an easy, rhythmic drawl"
faults.why: The lesson makes a broad stylistic contrast, but gives limited guidance about when to retain short sentences for comic timing or how to avoid merely adding archaic vocabulary. Its main reusable advice is confined to joining a list with "and".

faults.quote: "The writer's: setting ... an offish sister"
faults.why: The side-by-side structural account is meant to teach the writer how their original is built, but it silently substitutes the rewrite's repaired fact for the original fact, making the comparison unreliable.

judge.verdict: The rewrite sensibly addresses the supplied contradiction and retains the basic sequence, but it adds an unnecessary backstory, changes several concrete details, and reaches only a generalized faux-Twain voice. Its explanatory materials are weakened by inaccurately calling the original woman a sister and by an unsubstantiated source citation.

yours:
Hi team,

Quick update: the launch is moving from Tuesday to Thursday. Legal still hasn't signed off on the pricing page, and I don't want us shipping without it.

Please have your sections of the deck done by Wednesday at noon. If you're blocked, tell me today, not tomorrow.

Thanks,
Sam
rewrite:
To the team:

Here is a brief piece of information for you: the launch is put off, and will not take place on Tuesday, but on Thursday. The lawyers have not yet set their hands to the sheet of prices; and I am not minded that we should ship without their warrant.

Pray see to it, therefore, that your several parts of the papers are finished up by Wednesday at noon. If any man has run upon a snag, let him speak out to-day, and not wait upon to-morrow.

Yours with thanks, Sam.

rows.text: To the team:

Here is a brief piece of information for you: the launch is put off, and will not take place on Tuesday, but on Thursday. The lawyers have not yet set their hands to the sheet of prices; and I am not minded that we should ship without their warrant.

notes.text: The voice clarifies corporate sign-off as the lawyers' formal warrant or assent.
notes.after: without their warrant

rows.text: Pray see to it, therefore, that your several parts of the papers are finished up by Wednesday at noon. If any man has run upon a snag, let him speak out to-day, and not wait upon to-morrow.

notes.text: A modern presentation deck has no place in the nineteenth century, so the voice names it plainly by what it is: the papers.
notes.after: the papers

rows.text: Yours with thanks, Sam.

lessons: The chief difference lies in replacing clipped modern office jargon with Twain’s rhythmic, spoken phrasing and river-tested idiom. Notice how “Legal still hasn't signed off” becomes “The lawyers have not yet set their hands,” and being blocked turns into having “run upon a snag.” Practise using balanced clauses and plain Anglo-Saxon phrasing to give routine announcements weight and natural cadence.

outline.gist: Salutation to the team
Launch postponed from Tuesday to Thursday pending legal sign-off on pricing
Finish deck sections by Wednesday noon and report blockers immediately
Sign-off and thanks from Sam

plan.gist: Salutation to the team
plan.why: Keep the epistolary form, addressing the assembled company directly.

plan.gist: Launch postponed from Tuesday to Thursday pending legal sign-off on pricing
plan.why: Announce the delay first, followed immediately by the lawyers' hesitation as the plain reason.

plan.gist: Finish deck sections by Wednesday noon and report blockers immediately
plan.why: Set the deadline for the report, then conclude with an antithetical injunction against lingering until tomorrow.
A brief, courteous closing formula.
plan.gist: Sign-off and thanks from Sam

faults.quote: "your several parts of the papers"
faults.why: This replaces a presentation "deck" with generic "papers." A deck is not merely a collection of papers; it is a specific shared presentation artifact, so the revision loses precision.

faults.quote: "If any man has run upon a snag"
faults.why: The original addresses any team member. "Any man" unnecessarily narrows the addressee by gender and changes the inclusive office instruction.

faults.quote: "The lawyers have not yet set their hands to the sheet of prices"
faults.why: This turns legal approval of a particular "pricing page" into a physical or formal act concerning a "sheet of prices." The latter is less specific and does not clearly preserve the web-page/document context.

faults.quote: "Here is a brief piece of information for you"
faults.why: This is stiff, inflated administrative prose rather than Twain's characteristic directness, comic precision, or conversational economy. It reads as generic faux-period diction.

faults.quote: "Pray see to it, therefore"
faults.why: "Pray" and the ceremonious connective "therefore" are stock Victorian signals, not a persuasive imitation of Twain's usual American colloquial syntax.

faults.quote: "Yours with thanks, Sam."
faults.why: The closing is English-Victorian pastiche. It does not sound like Twain's distinct epistolary voice and is less natural than the original concise business sign-off.

faults.quote: "I am not minded that we should ship without their warrant"
faults.why: "Not minded that" is awkward in this construction, and "their warrant" is an unnatural way to refer to legal sign-off on a pricing page. It risks suggesting that shipping itself requires a legal warrant.

faults.quote: "let him speak out to-day, and not wait upon to-morrow"
faults.why: "Wait upon tomorrow" is strained and ambiguous: it can mean serving tomorrow rather than delaying until tomorrow. The hyphenated "to-day" further reads as costume rather than living idiom.

faults.quote: "Liberty taken: A modern presentation deck has no place in the nineteenth century"
faults.why: This inaccurately justifies a loss of meaning. The task is to render the writer's actual email in the voice, not to pretend the email's workplace object cannot exist. The note should acknowledge that "papers" broadens and weakens "deck," or retain the deck more precisely.

faults.quote: "The voice clarifies corporate sign-off as the lawyers' formal warrant or assent."
faults.why: The change does not clarify; "warrant" makes the legal condition less exact and introduces a different legal concept. The note also fails to identify the loss of the original's specific "pricing page."

faults.quote: "Paragraph 1: (no notes)"
faults.why: The first substantive paragraph makes several consequential stylistic and semantic changes, including "Quick update" becoming "Here is a brief piece of information" and the pricing page becoming a "sheet of prices," but these are not documented.

faults.quote: all notes
faults.why: The notes cite no Twain letters, sketches, novels, or other sources for the claimed stylistic moves, despite presenting assertions about what "the voice" would do.

faults.quote: "replacing clipped modern office jargon with Twain’s rhythmic, spoken phrasing and river-tested idiom"
faults.why: This is broad and impressionistic rather than a reusable lesson. It does not distinguish Twain's actual plain, vernacular directness from the rewrite's ornamental pseudo-archaic language.

faults.quote: "Practise using balanced clauses and plain Anglo-Saxon phrasing"
faults.why: The advice is not grounded in a specific structural choice from the email, and "plain Anglo-Saxon" contradicts much of the rewrite's diction, such as "information," "several," "formal," and "warrant." It gives the writer no concrete method for preserving modern business precision while changing cadence.

judge.verdict: The email preserves the broad sequence and the two requests, but it achieves its period effect chiefly through generic Victorian costume rather than Twain's recognizable voice. Its notes defend avoidable losses of precision and provide little reliable, transferable instruction.

yours:
Our town should close Main Street to cars on weekends. Parking downtown is a nightmare and the sidewalks are too narrow for strollers. Other towns have done this and their shops are doing better than ever.

Some business owners will complain that customers can't get to them. But they'll get used to it. Honestly, most people walk from the garage anyway.

We should try it this summer.
rewrite:
Our town ought to shut up Main Street against cars every Saturday and Sunday; for putting up a team downtown is a positive nightmare, and the sidewalks are a deal too narrow for baby carriages. They have tried the plan in other towns, and their shops are doing a handsome and brisker business today than ever they did before.

To be sure, some of the storekeepers will complain, and insist that customers cannot get to them. They will get used to it soon enough, I reckon; for honestly, most people walk from the stable anyway.

We ought to take hold and give the thing a trial this summer.

rows.text: Our town ought to shut up Main Street against cars every Saturday and Sunday; for putting up a team downtown is a positive nightmare, and the sidewalks are a deal too narrow for baby carriages. They have tried the plan in other towns, and their shops are doing a handsome and brisker business today than ever they did before.

To be sure, some of the storekeepers will complain, and insist that customers cannot get to them. They will get used to it soon enough, I reckon; for honestly, most people walk from the stable anyway.

notes.after: They will get used to it soon enough, I reckon;

notes.text: The vernacular voice frames the merchants’ complaint with an easy conversational concession before dismissing it.
notes.after: To be sure,

notes.text: The narrator qualifies the prediction with a characteristic conversational aside.
notes.after: I reckon

rows.text: We ought to take hold and give the thing a trial this summer.

lessons: Your draft made a sequence of short, clipped assertions; Twain links cause to effect in rolling cumulative sentences, joining your opening proposal to its practical reason with '; for putting up a team downtown is a positive nightmare, and the sidewalks are a deal too narrow for baby carriages.' He then punctures solemn objections not with elaborate debate, but with an offhand aside ('I reckon') and the flat, deadpan truth that 'for honestly, most people walk from the stable anyway.' Practise letting your civic arguments lean on easy spoken cadences and commonsense fact rather than brisk policy pronouncements.

outline.gist: close Main Street to cars on weekends
parking is a nightmare and sidewalks are too narrow for strollers
other towns have done this and shops do better
merchants will complain that customers cannot reach them
merchants will get used to it
people walk from the garage anyway
try it this summer

plan.why: Twain joins the opening claim to its immediate physical justification with a semicolon and 'for', building a rolling cumulative sentence.
plan.gist: close Main Street on weekends because parking is impossible and sidewalks are too narrow
other towns have tested it and their shops thrive
plan.why: A balanced declarative sentence supplies external confirmation that the plan succeeds in practice.
An informal concession sets the merchant complaint in place so it can be punctured.
plan.gist: business owners will grumble about lost access
merchants will adjust because customers walk from the stable anyway
plan.why: Coupling the forecast to a flat, deadpan fact lands the answer as plain common sense.

plan.gist: try the closure this summer
plan.why: A brief, plain close concludes the piece without inflated rhetoric.

faults.quote: “putting up a team downtown”
faults.why: This replaces the writer’s specific problem—parking cars downtown—with handling or stabling a horse-drawn team. It is not merely an archaic phrasing of parking, and shifts the setting and practical issue.

faults.quote: “most people walk from the stable anyway”
faults.why: The original says people walk from “the garage,” presumably a parking garage. A stable is a materially different place and introduces an unnecessary horse-and-carriage implication.

faults.quote: “for honestly, most people walk from the stable anyway”
faults.why: Because “stable” no longer clearly serves as the downtown parking garage in the writer’s argument, the answer to the merchants’ access objection is weakened and made less clear.

faults.quote: “their shops are doing a handsome and brisker business today than ever they did before”
faults.why: “Handsome” and comparative “brisker” do not coordinate naturally here: the phrase asks one business to be both handsome and ‘brisker’ without a corresponding comparison for “handsome.” The syntax sounds strained rather than idiomatically Twainian.

faults.quote: “for honestly, most people walk from the stable anyway”
faults.why: The horses-and-stable diction reads as a costume substitution for a modern civic argument, rather than Twain’s more exact, context-sensitive vernacular. Twain could write about teams and stables, but the language should not distort the actual modern object being discussed.

faults.quote: “Liberty taken: The vernacular voice frames the merchants’ complaint with an easy conversational concession before dismissing it.”
faults.why: This describes a stylistic maneuver, not a liberty that needed to be taken. More importantly, the notes omit the genuine factual liberties: changing cars to a “team” and a garage to a “stable.”

faults.quote: “the flat, deadpan truth that 'for honestly, most people walk from the stable anyway.'”
faults.why: The lesson endorses the altered detail as though it were the writer’s fact. It should disclose and justify a sense mending, or, better, retain “garage” and make the cadence Twain-like without changing the referent.

faults.quote: “cites Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, ch. 17, ¶ 59”
faults.why: The citation is too imprecise to be useful because paragraph numbering varies substantially by edition, and it does not identify what wording or syntactic move is being sourced. The note should quote the relevant Twain passage or use a stable chapter-and-phrase reference.

faults.quote: Paragraph 1: “(no notes)”
faults.why: The first paragraph contains the largest substantive transformations—“cars” to “team” and the parking problem’s reframing—but supplies no explanation of them.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the argument’s overall order and gives it a plausible colloquial nineteenth-century cadence, but its horse-and-stable substitutions alter concrete facts rather than merely recasting them. The teaching is usefully specific about cadence and concession, yet the notes fail to acknowledge the consequential changes they make.

yours:
I think we should switch to a four-day week. People are burned out and our best engineer just quit. There are studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up. It would also help with hiring.

I know it's risky and clients might not like it. We could try it for three months and see.
rewrite:
I judge we would do well to knock off work after four days of it in every week; for the men are clean wore out, and our best engineer has up and quit on us already. Besides, the printed reports go to show that the work turned out stays right where it was, or even goes higher; and it would give us a mighty lift in getting new hands into the shop, too.

I know there is a risk in it, and the customers may take it hard at first, but we could make a trial of it for three months and see how it works.

rows.text: I judge we would do well to knock off work after four days of it in every week; for the men are clean wore out, and our best engineer has up and quit on us already. Besides, the printed reports go to show that the work turned out stays right where it was, or even goes higher; and it would give us a mighty lift in getting new hands into the shop, too.
I know there is a risk in it, and the customers may take it hard at first, but we could make a trial of it for three months and see how it works.

lessons: Twain replaces modern managerial jargon with plain vernacular cadence, turning the flat plea for a four-day week into a deliberate, cumulative argument built on observation and deadpan balance. Instead of quoting abstract "productivity studies," the voice relies on a folksy aside ("which is plain enough to anybody that has watched a man work") and strings the consequences together with rhythmic "and"s.

outline.gist: Proposal to work four days and reasons why
Risk, client concern, and a trial period

plan.why: Twain begins with a practical verdict stated in vernacular terms and immediately backs it with human evidence before turning to figures or logic.
plan.gist: Proposal and immediate human reasons

plan.why: Twain balances risk against plain experience, concluding with a sensible, measured test rather than abstract debate.
plan.gist: Acknowledge objections and propose practical trial

faults.quote: the men are clean wore out
faults.why: “People” is narrowed to “men,” unnecessarily changing the stated group and making the proposal gender-exclusive.

faults.quote: our best engineer has up and quit on us already
faults.why: “Already” adds an implication that the resignation occurred sooner than expected or as a warning already realized; the original only says the engineer “just quit.”

faults.quote: the printed reports go to show
faults.why: The evidence is changed from “studies” to “printed reports.” Studies may be printed, but “reports” is not the same stated evidentiary category and weakens precision.

faults.quote: getting new hands into the shop
faults.why: “Into the shop” imports an industrial/workshop setting not supplied by the writer. The original only says the policy would help with hiring.

faults.quote: the customers may take it hard at first
faults.why: “At first” invents a prediction that clients will later cease objecting. The draft merely says they “might not like it.”

faults.quote: knock off work after four days of it in every week
faults.why: This is broad, costume-like folksiness rather than a particularly Twain-like turn. It is more labor vernacular than Twain’s characteristic pointed, comic precision.

faults.quote: knock off work after four days of it in every week
faults.why: The phrasing is clumsy and mildly ambiguous: it can sound like everyone simply stops work after four days, rather than that the organization adopts a recurring four-day workweek.

faults.quote: new hands into the shop
faults.why: The stock rustic-industrial diction feels imposed to signal an old-time voice, especially beside the modern office-specific fact of an “engineer.”

faults.quote: (no notes)
faults.why: The rewrite makes several substantive lexical and framing changes, but the notes identify none of them. In particular, they do not disclose or justify the changed evidence label (“studies” to “printed reports”) or the added shop setting.

faults.quote: which is plain enough to anybody that has watched a man work
faults.why: The lesson attributes this quoted aside to the rewrite, but that sentence does not appear in it. This makes the teaching note inaccurate.

faults.quote: strings the consequences together with rhythmic "and"s
faults.why: The lesson overstates a technique that is not meaningfully developed in the rewrite; it gives the writer no exact, reliable account of the actual revisions.

faults.quote: Twain replaces modern managerial jargon with plain vernacular cadence
faults.why: This is too general to be a reusable lesson, and it misdescribes “studies showing productivity stays the same or goes up” as mere managerial jargon rather than evidence that must be retained accurately.

judge.verdict: The argument’s original order and all major points are largely retained, but the Twain effect relies on generic rustic diction and introduces several avoidable shifts in scope and implication. The absent notes and inaccurate lesson substantially undermine the piece’s value as a teaching tool.

yours:
When Dana cancelled our dinner I wasn't upset at all. Honestly, I was relieved. I'd been dreading it all week, and I'm not proud of that.

I told her it was fine and we'd do it another time. I don't think we will.
rewrite:
When Dana sent word she could not take dinner with me, I was not put out in the least; to tell the honest truth, I was considerably relieved. It is no great credit to a man, I judge, but I had dreaded the business the whole week through.

I told her it was all right, of course, and that we would manage it some other time. I do not reckon we ever will.

rows.text: When Dana sent word she could not take dinner with me, I was not put out in the least; to tell the honest truth, I was considerably relieved. It is no great credit to a man, I judge, but I had dreaded the business the whole week through.

notes.after: It is no great credit to a man, I judge
notes.cite: Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc, ch. 52, ¶ 5

notes.text: The voice takes the narrator's private sheepishness and frames it as a dry, generalized verdict on human nature.
notes.after: It is no great credit to a man, I judge

rows.text: I told her it was all right, of course, and that we would manage it some other time. I do not reckon we ever will.

lessons: Where your draft relies on clipped, modern assertions, Twain leans into rhythmic, balanced periods and vernacular ease. Notice how joining the cancellation to the confession across a semicolon in “When Dana sent word she could not take dinner with me, I was not put out in the least; to tell the honest truth, I was considerably relieved” allows the secret satisfaction to land with full weight, while closing on the flat, deadpan dismissal “I do not reckon we ever will” lets the comic truth sit without need of explanation. Practise letting your narrator confess private, unflattering truths in an unhurried voice and trusting the short punchline to finish the work.

outline.gist: Dana cancels dinner and the narrator is not upset.
The narrator confesses to feeling relieved.
The narrator admits to dreading it all week and feeling sheepish about that.
The narrator smoothly lies and agrees to reschedule.
The narrator doubts they will ever actually meet.

plan.gist: Dana puts off dinner and the narrator confesses relief.
plan.why: Twain joins the cancellation to the immediate sense of relief in a single balanced sentence, using the semicolon to pivot from social expectation to frank confession.

plan.gist: The narrator confesses the week of dread with dry self-reproach.
plan.why: He frames the shameful feeling through an aside, making conscience sound like plain, humorous common sense.
He carries off the conventional social pretense in smooth, easy narrative rhythm.
plan.gist: Politely agreeing to reschedule another time.

plan.why: A short, deadpan closing period lands the punchline without comment or apology.
plan.gist: The flat dismissal of the future dinner.

faults.quote: "It is no great credit to a man, I judge"
faults.why: This introduces a male narrator where the original gives no gender. It also turns a private admission of not being proud into a generalized judgment about what deserves a man's credit; the direction of feeling remains intact, but the meaning is somewhat broadened.

faults.quote: "I was considerably relieved"
faults.why: "Considerably" makes the relief more emphatic than the original's plain "I was relieved." The original's "Honestly" supplies frankness, not necessarily a stronger degree of relief.

faults.quote: "I had dreaded the business"
faults.why: Calling the dinner "the business" adds a faintly transactional or burdensome characterization not explicit in the writer's wording. It is not a major invention, but it is an extra gloss on the event.

faults.quote: "not put out in the least" / "to tell the honest truth" / "I do not reckon"
faults.why: These are plausible period-flavored markers, but stacked together they produce a generalized, costume-Twain sound rather than a distinctive Twainian comic movement or observation. The passage relies chiefly on familiar dialect signals rather than demonstrating his more particular tonal surprises and precision.

faults.quote: "to a man"
faults.why: The added gendered phrase creates an otherwise unnecessary question about the narrator's identity. The original is clear without it, and the rewrite should not narrow an unspecified speaker.

faults.quote: "frames it as a dry, generalized verdict on human nature"
faults.why: The cited move does not quite do what this note says: "to a man" is a judgment about the narrator or men generally, not a verdict on "human nature." More importantly, the note does not acknowledge that this liberty adds a gendered narrator and broadens the original's strictly personal shame.

faults.quote: "The narrator smoothly lies and agrees to reschedule"
faults.why: The writer says the narrator told Dana it was fine and that they would do it another time, then privately doubts it will happen. That permits social politeness or pessimism, but does not establish a lie. The structural account invents an intention to deceive.

faults.quote: "the conventional social pretense"
faults.why: This repeats the unsupported claim that the narrator's response was knowingly false. The original does not say whether Dana, the narrator, or circumstances will prevent the later dinner; "I don't think we will" is not proof of pretense.

faults.quote: "Where your draft relies on clipped, modern assertions"
faults.why: This overstates the contrast. The original's short, direct sentences are a deliberate and effective fit for its restrained confession; calling them merely a limitation risks teaching the writer to replace a working native strength with period-style padding.

faults.quote: "letting your narrator confess private, unflattering truths in an unhurried voice"
faults.why: This is a usable general exercise, but it does not address the most consequential interpretive choice in the rewrite: whether the polite promise is a lie, a convention, or simply an uncertain future plan. A stronger lesson would distinguish deadpan implication from asserting motives not supplied by the draft.

judge.verdict: The rewrite preserves the sequence and emotional direction well and remains readable, but it adds a gendered generalization and the accompanying teaching materials overread the narrator's polite response as a lie. Its Twain effect is competent but largely assembled from familiar period markers rather than strongly distinctive Twainian prose.
